The authors say this relaxes strict unitarity so the device can be reconfigured more easily while still behaving close to an ideal unitary transformation. They report a normalized mean square error of about 0.0023 on the prediction task and a drop in average bit error rate from 0.9 to 0.0018 on the fiber-distortion task. The core occupies 0.65 mm by 2.15 mm, and the authors project 102.4 TOPS at 42.1 TOPS per watt if the chip is paired with 50 GHz modulators, a figure they have not yet measured.

The authors argue that conventional Mach-Zehnder interferometer meshes become hard to scale because their component count grows with the square of matrix size, and that their approach offers a more compact alternative. The preprint describes the work as a route to scalable, energy-efficient on-chip photonic computing. The articles provided do not name the authors or their institutions, and they do not say whether the work has been independently verified. They also do not describe any planned publication or next steps beyond the preprint itself.

Articles.Title: Reconfigurable Photonic Quasi-Unitary Computing Hardware for Optical Signal Processing

stories.Headline: Surviving the Router: Optimizing Skill Injections for Retrieval and Execution
stories.Summary:
Researchers Haneen Najjar, Luca Scionis, Haritz Puerto and Sahar Abdelnabi posted a paper on arXiv, reported October 24, 2026, about attacks on AI agents that rely on third-party "skills" chosen by a skill router. The paper argues that earlier studies of prompt injections hidden in these skills assumed the malicious skill had already been selected for execution. The authors say that assumption can greatly overstate how often such attacks succeed. They report that in realistic multi-skill environments, injected skills must first compete to be retrieved, which cuts the attack success rate of existing injections by 87 to 97 percent.

To address this, the authors introduce CORSA, short for Cluster Optimization for Router-Aware Skill Attacks, a method that tailors skill injections to the router. CORSA works in successive stages, first improving how often an injected skill is retrieved and then optimizing end-to-end attack success across clusters of related tasks. The authors tested it by extending the SkillRouter benchmark with eight malicious payload categories. They assessed user utility and injection naturalism separately from the attack results. The article describes these tests only at this level of detail and does not give further figures.

According to the abstract, the experiments show that CORSA substantially improves both retrieval and end-to-end attack success over existing skill injections while still preserving user utility. The authors also say the resulting attacks transfer across different router architectures and different LLM backbones. The paper is presented as research on the vulnerability of agent systems rather than as a report of an incident in deployed products. The source text does not describe any specific responses from router or model developers, nor any planned changes to skill selection systems.

Articles.Title: Surviving the Router: Optimizing Skill Injections for Retrieval and Execution

stories.Headline: DLoop: Looped Speculative Decoding
stories.Summary:
Researchers Geonmo Gu, Byeongho Heo, HeeJae Jun, Yoohoon Kang, Sangmin Lee, Sangdoo Yun, and Dongyoon Han have published a paper introducing DLoop, a looped form of speculative decoding, which was posted on October 24, 2026. Speculative decoding speeds up text generation in large language models by having a lightweight draft model propose tokens that a larger target model then checks. The authors observed that the target model often accepts every token a draft stage produces, yet a verification step still follows each stage, which forces target-model forward passes that could have been avoided. Existing adaptive draft length methods help only with autoregressive draft models, not with parallel draft models.

DLoop changes this process by letting the system run multiple drafting stages before any verification takes place. Drafting continues while the draft model remains confident, and all accumulated draft tokens are then verified together. To keep the draft model reliable across these extra stages, the authors use loop-aware training, which exposes the model to its own hidden states for tokens that have not yet been verified. The extra draft-model passes reduce the number of target-model passes needed for verification. The paper reports that across methods including EAGLE-3, DFlash, Domino, DSpark, and multi-token prediction modules, DLoop improves wall-clock speedup by 5 to 41 percent while preserving lossless decoding.

The paper is credited to the seven named authors, and the source material does not describe any institutional affiliation or further responsibility beyond that. The authors state that code will be made available at a link given in the paper. The article does not describe any peer review, publication venue, or independent evaluation of the results. It also does not say how DLoop will be adopted or what follow-up work the team plans.

Articles.Title: DLoop: Looped Speculative Decoding

stories.Headline: Learning consistent molecular mechanics force fields from first principles
stories.Summary:
A research team has posted a preprint describing a new method for building molecular mechanics force fields, the simplified models used to run large-scale molecular simulations. The paper, titled "Learning consistent molecular mechanics force fields from first principles," was authored by Berkay Günes, Leif Seute, Jigyasa Nigam and Frauke Gräter and was listed on arXiv with an October 24, 2026 timestamp. The authors say classical force fields remain the main tool for large simulations even as machine-learned interatomic potentials come close to ab initio accuracy. Traditional force fields assign their parameters based on atom or bond types, which keeps simulations efficient but limits how well they adapt across different molecular configurations.

The authors introduce a unified approach, called grappa-fullFF, that learns both bonded and nonbonded parameters together from ab initio reference data. Earlier machine learning work had improved bonded parameters but still depended on empirical nonbonded parameters for practical simulations, which the new method avoids. The model adds physically inspired regularization through supervision of the electrostatic potential, along with an architecture designed to support charge equilibration. According to the abstract, this allows the model to recover accurate electric response properties and reach state-of-the-art accuracy on geometry optimization benchmarks.

It also reproduces the conformational sampling of both classical and existing machine-learned force fields without relying on externally assigned nonbonded parameters. The work is the product of the four named authors, and the abstract's own language describes the results as claims that remain to be checked by the wider community. The paper is categorized under chemical physics, machine learning and computational physics on arXiv. The articles supplied do not describe peer review, funding, institutional affiliations, or any planned follow-up work, so what happens next beyond the posting itself is not stated.

Articles.Title: Learning consistent molecular mechanics force fields from first principles

stories.Headline: TRACE: Rollout-Guided Quantization-Aware Training for FP4 Reinforcement Learning of MoE Language Models
stories.Summary:
The paper TRACE, posted to arXiv and listed by doi.org on October 24, 2026, describes a new method for training large language models with 4-bit floating-point precision. The authors are Xin Wang, Hao Yu, Zhengyang Zhuge, Bochao Mao, Zheng Li, Junda Feng, Yuyan Luo, Yi Zhang, Yizhong Cao, Mi Zhang, Dayiheng Liu and Jianwei Zhang, who together submitted the work as a research preprint. The abstract says reinforcement learning for post-training large language models requires heavy computation and memory during rollout generation, which is why low-precision rollouts are attractive. The paper argues that existing FP4 reinforcement learning methods optimize quantization on the training and rollout paths separately rather than reducing the gap between them.

TRACE, short for Train-Rollout Quantization Alignment via Compact GuidancE, is presented as an FP4 framework for reinforcement learning of Mixture-of-Experts language models. It uses rollout-side quantization outcomes to guide rounding decisions on the training side, which the authors say directly narrows the discrepancy between the two paths. It also adds a caching scheme that keeps only selected mantissa and scale information from deeper layers, aiming to cut the storage and communication costs that the rollout guidance introduces. The authors say they tested the method on four large-scale Mixture-of-Experts models across reasoning, coding and long-horizon reinforcement learning tasks.

According to the abstract, TRACE allows joint FP4 weight and activation rollouts together with FP4 KV-cache rollouts. The authors report reinforcement learning performance comparable to rollouts run in BF16, along with rollout speedups of up to 5.4 times. They also say the method yields stronger final FP4 performance than applying post-hoc FP4 quantization to policies trained in BF16. The paper is an arXiv preprint, so these results have not been described as peer-reviewed in the material provided, and the article text gives no further details on who funded the work or what follows next.

Articles.Title: TRACE: Rollout-Guided Quantization-Aware Training for FP4 Reinforcement Learning of MoE Language Models

stories.Headline: Is Yoo Jae-suk curious about his financial luck, too? AI saju ‘draws attention’ (Running Man)
stories.Summary:
A short clip of Yoo Jae-suk having his financial luck read has drawn attention ahead of the SBS variety show "Running Man." The episode airing on the 25th follows the members on an outing in Jongno 3-ga, where they compete to avoid paying out of pocket for activities and lunch. The race is a "corporate card odyssey," in which members who do not secure a corporate card must cover every expense that day with their personal cards. The area was ranked No. 1 on Time Out's list of the world's coolest neighborhoods and has been featured by CNN.

Early in the day, the members tried a "hyeokpil painting," a form of letter drawing in which multicolored letters and images are layered with a firm leather brush to depict names. To celebrate the upcoming wedding of youngest member Ji Ye-eun, they requested her name, and the resulting artwork left the members speechless, according to reports. Afterward, the group visited a cafe offering AI readings of saju and physiognomy. When Yoo Jae-suk tried to check his financial luck first, the other members objected together, and curiosity has built over how his results turned out.

At lunch, the members faced a dish they were unfamiliar with, deokja-jjim, which measured a full 50 cm, and only five people could eat. To decide who would pay, they laid out their personal and corporate cards in a row and moved a measuring tape, with the card where it stopped being the one used to pay. Ji Ye-eun's card was selected, and she then had to name a member to be excluded from the meal with her, which sparked a playful argument. Yoo Jae-suk and Kim Jong-kook, who are set to emcee and sing at the wedding, joked that they should be spared, drawing laughs.

Articles.Title: Is Yoo Jae-suk curious about his financial luck, too? AI saju ‘draws attention’ (Running Man)

stories.Headline: A Human-AI Collaborative Workflow for Mathematical Discovery: A Case Study in Grover-Compatible Riemannian Optimization
stories.Summary:
The articles available describe a single Springer Nature paper, published on 24 October 2026 in the Journal of Scientific Computing, titled "A Human-AI Collaborative Workflow for Mathematical Discovery: A Case Study in Grover-Compatible Riemannian Optimization." The authors, listed with ORCID identifiers and including Dong An, Jiang Hu and Zaiwen Wen, describe a human-in-the-loop workflow in which experts keep control of problem formulation and assumptions while large language models search for proofs or contradictions, propose candidate properties and theorems, and help build structures and parameters that meet explicit constraints. The model's outputs are supported by numerical experiments and simple verification checks, and human experts then refine them into precise statements and rigorous proofs. The paper says the workflow was applied to a main case study connecting manifold optimization with Grover's quantum search algorithm, where it identified invariant subspaces and explored Grover-compatible retractions.

The paper also relies on a companion mathematical work, a Grover-compatible manifold optimization algorithm by Lai, An, Hu and Wen, which establishes an O(√N log(1/ε)) convergence bound under a Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition. The authors state that prompt records and reusable templates for implementing the workflow are publicly available in a GitHub repository. The paper additionally includes a multi-oracle case study, documents representative failed and corrected routes, and provides a structured failure-mode analysis. The articles do not say how the workflow would be adopted beyond this study, nor do they give any further results beyond those summarized.

The authors present the workflow as a way for LLMs to serve as research tools in scientific computing while preserving mathematical rigor, with the human expert retaining final responsibility for the statements and proofs. The abstract frames the model's role as producing raw material that experts then check and organize, rather than as an independent source of proofs. The paper's reference list places it among a growing body of work on AI-assisted theorem proving, conjecture generation and automated research, including efforts from DeepMind, OpenAI and academic groups. The articles do not indicate any planned follow-up work or next steps beyond the publication itself.

Articles.Title: A Human-AI Collaborative Workflow for Mathematical Discovery: A Case Study in Grover-Compatible Riemannian Optimization

stories.Headline: CVIF: A Criticality-Driven Visual Intervention Framework for Geometric Diagram Understanding in MLLMs
stories.Summary:
A team of seven researchers, led by Jiahui Kang, posted a paper describing CVIF, a training-free framework for helping multimodal large language models read geometric diagrams. The paper appeared on the arXiv preprint server, with the record showing a date of October 24, 2026. The researchers say these models often struggle with geometric diagrams because such images contain sparse visual cues and ambiguous links between symbols and the shapes they label. As a result, the models may lean on text-based assumptions and give answers that contradict what the diagram actually shows.

CVIF works at inference time, meaning it changes how a model responds during use rather than requiring retraining. The method finds critical layers in the model, the points where it moves from gathering visual evidence to producing its interpretation. At those layers, a module called GCLR selects and weights evidence centered on the diagram's vertices, and a second component called AVSO shifts the model's attention toward the selected visual tokens. The authors tested the approach on two benchmark datasets, PGPS9K and PGDP5K.

According to the abstract, CVIF raised the Overall F1 score from 77.85 to 85.58 on PGPS9K and from 75.23 to 82.84 on PGDP5K. The authors describe the work as establishing a new paradigm for inference-time visual intervention. The paper is a preprint and had not been described in the materials as peer reviewed. The articles provided do not say whether the authors plan further releases, code, or follow-up studies.

Articles.Title: CVIF: A Criticality-Driven Visual Intervention Framework for Geometric Diagram Understanding in MLLMs

stories.Headline: MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a research paper, not a news event, so there is no reported incident, no named actor beyond the authors, and no date beyond the posting timestamp of October 24, 2026. The paper, titled MemPilot, was posted on the arXiv repository and comes from nine researchers including Haozhen Zhang, Haodong Yue, and Wenya Wang. It presents a framework for managing memory in large language model agents, meaning the systems that retain and reuse information across interactions. The authors say most existing systems build memory without regard to the specific query, which can waste preprocessing effort and discard details that later turn out to matter.

According to the abstract, MemPilot instead curates memory on demand, using a multi-step policy trained with reinforcement learning. At each step the policy chooses between retrieving from general stored memory and asking other language models or vision-language models to curate the raw multimodal history for the current query. The policy also controls how much evidence is gathered, what curation instructions are given, which model is selected, and whether visual content is accessed. To balance competing goals, the authors describe a method for estimating each objective's advantage separately before combining them, along with a prefix-based way of assigning credit across multi-step rollouts.

The authors report experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks and state that MemPilot achieves favorable trade-offs among performance, cost, and latency across different optimization preferences. They say preference sweeps produce broader performance frontiers than existing trade-off-aware baselines. The abstract does not describe deployment, release of code, or any next steps beyond the posted findings. The work sits within the broader effort to make LLM agents more efficient, since the authors frame runtime adaptation as an area that prior studies had explored only in narrow or fixed forms.

Articles.Title: MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents

stories.Headline: RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
stories.Summary:
The arXiv preprint "RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents" was posted on doi.org on 24 October 2026, with eight authors led by Mohamed Dhouib. The paper addresses indirect prompt injection, in which tool-using language-model agents act on untrusted external content and can be manipulated by instructions hidden in it. The authors report that existing training-time defenses can lower attack success rates but often reduce the model's general capabilities. They present RAISED, a training framework that combines self-generation and self-distillation as a response.

According to the abstract, the authors found that training-based defenses cause substantial drift in the model's output distribution, which changes its behavior even in benign settings and may explain the loss of utility. They also found that on benign tool-use tasks, a model trained this way sometimes refuses a step needed to finish an authorized task, especially when a tool output indicates that step. Under RAISED, the model first generates its own tool-use scenarios, emphasizing cases where finishing the task depends on acting on legitimate guidance from tool outputs. The student model is then trained through self-distillation to match the teacher's clean-context behavior on both clean and injected versions of the same trajectory. The abstract does not give specific figures for the reduction in attack success rates.

The paper is credited to Mohamed Dhouib, Clement Elliker, Alexi Canesse, Maël Jenny, Lucas-Andrei Thil, Mahammed El Sharkawy, Sonia Vanier and Elie Bursztein. The authors state that RAISED substantially reduces attack success rates for prompt injections in tool responses while preserving performance on both agentic and general-purpose benchmarks, unlike prior training-based defenses. The preprint is categorized under cryptography and security, artificial intelligence, computation and language, and machine learning. The available material describes a preprint and does not indicate any peer-review status, deployment or next steps beyond the authors' reported results.

Articles.Title: RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents

stories.Headline: Science Edge Evaluation: SEE the Missing Step Toward Real Scientific Discovery
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to Research Square on October 24, 2026, introduces a benchmark called Science Edge Evaluation, or SEE, designed to test whether large language models can support real laboratory science. The benchmark consists of expert-curated multimodal questions drawn from peer-reviewed literature and experimental practice in chemistry, biology, and materials science. The authors evaluated 18 multimodal large language models on SEE, and even the best-performing model reached only 48.7 percent accuracy. The study also found that general-purpose models, on average, outperformed models specialized for science.

The authors report that giving models access to tools raised the best score in their visual-agent evaluation to 52.7 percent. They argue that tool use can widen the information available to a model but does not by itself produce reliable scientific reasoning. The central difficulty, in their account, is whether a model can keep information gathered from tools within the limits of the original experimental evidence. Their conclusion is that current models cannot yet reliably draw justified, evidence-bounded inferences from experimental results, a capability they describe as essential to real scientific discovery. Bridging that gap, they write, requires models to move beyond explaining established concepts toward deriving new, evidence-based insights from experimental data.

The article names the study's authors only in the supporting material, and the excerpt provided does not identify them by name or institution. The preprint is marked as not yet peer reviewed by a journal, and the authors declare no competing interests. The excerpt does not say whether the authors plan to release the benchmark publicly or how the findings will be followed up. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Science Edge Evaluation: SEE the Missing Step Toward Real Scientific Discovery

stories.Headline: Accuracy of a respiratory assessment chatbot in a nationwide messaging system for layperson diagnosis and triage: a randomized preregistered study
stories.Summary:
A randomized study published on October 24, 2026 in Nature Health tested LungDiag, a respiratory assessment chatbot built on GPT-4o and delivered through WeChat, against ordinary mobile web search for lay people. The trial ran from April to June 2025 and enrolled 2,400 adults without formal medical training at 24 Chinese healthcare systems, who were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio. In the main analysis of 2,176 questionnaires, 1,088 per group, the researchers measured item-level accuracy across risk and aetiology identification, preliminary diagnosis and triage. Participants were given simulated cases, and the work was described as prospective, non-interventional, multicentre and single-blind.

The chatbot scored higher on overall accuracy, at 70.0% against 55.4% for the control group, a difference of 14.6 percentage points with a 95% confidence interval of 12.2 to 17.0 points. The largest gap appeared in diagnosis items, where accuracy was 81.2% for LungDiag and 54.5% for search, while triage gains were smaller, at 53.4% against 47.1%. LungDiag took longer to complete, with a median of 527 seconds compared with 461 seconds. For binary high-urgency triage, LungDiag showed sensitivity of 85.6% and specificity of 62.1%, while the control group reached 80.9% and 56.0%. The authors note that the study does not establish effects on real-world care-seeking, diagnostic delay or clinical outcomes.

The article is written by a team led by J. He, the corresponding author, who can be contacted at the email address given in the paper. The authors have placed de-identified participant-level datasets and analysis code in a public GitHub repository and an archived Zenodo release, while keeping the chatbot's proprietary prompts, retrieval settings and knowledge layer private. Researchers wanting controlled access to those protected materials may request it from the corresponding author, with responses normally expected within four to six weeks. The paper's reference list places the work within a wider literature on AI in respiratory care, self-triage and clinical decision support.

Articles.Title: Accuracy of a respiratory assessment chatbot in a nationwide messaging system for layperson diagnosis and triage: a randomized preregistered study

stories.Headline: Jung Yeon-tae’s Professional GPT Revolution 8 | NVIDIA’s Vision for the AI Industrial Revolution
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA's GTC technology event in Berlin on October 21, 2026, focused on a shift in artificial intelligence from systems that answer questions toward systems that act in the physical world. The company's chief executive, Jensen Huang, said Europe's strengths in precision machinery, automobiles, and manufacturing could become a new source of industrial competitiveness when combined with AI. Several developments were highlighted, including robotics that goes beyond understanding language to perceiving surroundings and manipulating objects, a move toward integrated humanoid robot development platforms, and growing competition in data centers based on deployment speed and operating efficiency. Each announcement was presented as a company goal or plan rather than a verified result.

NVIDIA introduced DSX POD, a modular system meant to be assembled and tested in factories before being installed on site. The company said it could shorten deployment at a prepared location from about six months to as little as 14 days, but it described this as a target under specific conditions and not a verified average. Germany's Agile Robots, working with NVIDIA, plans to produce between 1,000 and 2,000 compact humanoid robots in 2027. NVIDIA also said it had committed about $10 billion in investment or support to Europe's technology ecosystem and was working with more than 12,000 partners, though the articles note this does not mean the full sum has already been spent as cash. For South Korea, the articles say these developments create opportunities in its strong semiconductor, automobile, electronics, shipbuilding, construction, and robotics industries, while also raising concerns about dependence on NVIDIA's ecosystem, uncertain returns on AI spending, rising energy demand, labor disruption, data sovereignty, and technological security.

Agile Robots is developing the Agile ONE S and Agile ONE SN, with the SN model using NVIDIA's Jetson Thor computing technology and GR00T-based AI development tools. According to Reuters, the robots stand about 1.4 meters tall and weigh around 34 kilograms, and are aimed at research institutions and companies. Agile Robots said production would start in late 2026, while NVIDIA's materials describe the SN model as a reference platform for research and development with availability planned for early 2027. The articles frame NVIDIA's aim as offering a standard platform that spares robotics researchers the work of building hardware and software integration from scratch, rather than the production volume itself.

The broader context, according to the analysis, is that the American-centered AI industry is facing competition from China's investments in models, chips, and robotics, while Europe holds major industrial firms such as Siemens, Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen, ABB, and Schneider Electric that could combine their manufacturing data with AI. The articles caution that physical AI carries higher stakes than text generation, since a wrong physical action can cause accidents or damage, making safety, emergency stopping, and traceable records central requirements. They also warn that fully general-purpose humanoid robots have not been perfected and face challenges in battery life, fine manipulation, fault recovery, and cost. Commercial use is therefore expected to start with research platforms and structured tasks before expanding gradually.

Articles.Title: Jung Yeon-tae’s Professional GPT Revolution 8 | NVIDIA’s Vision for the AI Industrial Revolution

stories.Headline: ARC Prize rejects OpenAI's claim that Astra scored 99.9 percent on AGI test
stories.Summary:
ARC Prize, the group behind the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, has rejected a claim by OpenAI that its GPT-6 Astra model scored 99.9 percent on the test. OpenAI touted that figure when it released the model on September 3, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang cited it days later in a post on X declaring that AGI had arrived. When ARC Prize ran Astra through its own neutral testing setup, the model scored 62.7 percent, still the highest result on the benchmark but far below the figure OpenAI and Huang promoted. The Huang post had passed 10 million views by Monday morning, according to TheNextWeb.

ARC Prize found that the 99.9 percent score came from a custom "tools-enabled" setup built by OpenAI, which lets the model keep its reasoning state across actions in a way the standard test does not. That configuration cost nearly $19,000 to run. ARC Prize said the score is not valid because other labs' models are not measured under those conditions. Running Astra through the same setup used for GPT-5.6, Gemini 4 Argon, or Claude Opus 5 would lower the number by more than 37 points. The ARC Prize benchmark was first released on March 25, 2026, when frontier models scored near zero against humans, who solved the same environments every time.

The organizers of the test and OpenAI are the parties at the center of the dispute. OpenAI revised five of the published benchmark figures after its launch post went up, and ARC Prize has declined to describe Astra's progress as AGI. The article says that scores on the benchmark have risen mainly because of better software wrapped around existing models, not because the models themselves got smarter. An open-source harness called Prime Agent lifted public scores from about 30 percent to over 95 percent on the same class of model by early October. Separately, a team of five Nvidia engineers reportedly reached 100 percent with Claude Opus 5 by rebuilding its surrounding software layer.

The dispute matters to the broader AI investment story because companies such as CoreWeave and Nvidia are justifying large infrastructure spending partly on the belief that general intelligence is near. Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, according to Bloomberg, no longer agree on the term or on a timeline, and they do not share a testable benchmark. ARC Prize has said it expects scores to keep rising through the rest of 2026 as more labs adopt harness techniques like Prime Agent's. The articles leave open whether those gains will count as progress toward AGI or only as better engineering around the same underlying model.

Articles.Title: ARC Prize rejects OpenAI's claim that Astra scored 99.9 percent on AGI test

stories.Headline: Adobe and NVIDIA open ICNX 2026 as generative AI reshapes production - K-EnterTech Hub

stories.Headline: Justice for People in the AI Economy Through Mass Litigation
stories.Summary:
Apple agreed to pay $250 million to settle class action claims that it sold the iPhone 16 and certain iPhone 15 models on the strength of "Apple Intelligence" features that plaintiffs say were never delivered. The claims arise in Landsheft v. Apple Inc. in the Northern District of California, where plaintiffs alleged that Apple promised an enhanced AI Siri able to draw on a user's personal context across applications. The court granted preliminary approval of the settlement on July 17, 2026. If the court grants final approval next year, the recovery would be the largest pure false advertising class action settlement in history.

The case shows that ordinary false advertising law can reach claims about what an AI product can do. Apple did not admit to any wrongdoing, and the settlement came before any court finding that it had engaged in the alleged conduct. The article notes that regulators have been slower to act, and in one example the Federal Trade Commission in December 2025 set aside its own 2024 order against Rytr LLC, an AI writing assistant it had alleged enabled fake consumer reviews. The FTC reportedly said the complaint failed to state a valid claim and that the order was too burdensome for AI innovation. Private litigation has therefore stepped into the gap that regulators have left.

A separate case, Bartone v. Meta Platforms, Inc., was filed on March 4, 2026 in the Northern District of California by the Clarkson Law Firm. Plaintiffs allege that Meta and Luxottica marketed AI glasses as "designed for privacy, controlled by you" while routing captured footage to offshore data annotators who reviewed and labelled consumers' videos. The article says Meta ended its subcontract with the data annotation provider in April 2026 after whistleblower accounts emerged. Regulators in the European Union, Kenya and the United Kingdom have reportedly opened inquiries.

The article presents these cases as part of a wider pattern in which AI harms are proliferating faster than regulators can respond. It points to other emerging areas of litigation, including individualised AI pricing that may use protected characteristics and algorithmic collusion between competitors. It also describes a July 2026 MIT and Carnegie Mellon study finding that only 11% of S&P 500 companies had deeply integrated AI by 2025, while companies talked about AI at roughly seven times the rate they used it. The authors frame mass actions as a key tool for ensuring that innovation does not come at the expense of individual rights and public safety.

Articles.Title: Justice for People in the AI Economy Through Mass Litigation - ICLG

stories.Headline: New England’s old buildings and old data centers could be upgraded to handle AI computing
stories.Summary:
Old data centers across New England, some of them decades old, could be retrofitted to handle artificial intelligence computing, according to a special New England News Collaborative series reported by Áine Pennello of Connecticut Public Radio on October 23, 2026. The clearest example is a data center in Trumbull, Connecticut, which has operated since the 1960s and is now in the middle of an upgrade from conventional computing to AI computing. Retrofitting means renovating an existing building instead of constructing a new one so it can supply the power and cooling that AI chips need. Local residents have raised concerns, and the article makes clear that these changes are hard to see from outside and difficult for opponents to stop.

The shift requires swapping the older central processing units, which are the core chips found in ordinary laptops, for graphics processing units, which handle far more data. According to Kenneth Gillingham, a professor of environmental and energy economics at Yale School of the Environment, these GPUs use two to three times more energy and run hotter than the older chips. He described operators pulling out the old CPUs and installing large numbers of GPUs, effectively replacing what is inside the facilities. The article also notes that Trumbull passed a two-year moratorium on new data centers last month, but that the ban does not stop the existing facility from being converted. A separate one-year moratorium proposal that would have limited increases in capacity was rejected by the town's planning and zoning commission on Wednesday, which said its language was too vague to enforce.

The companies leading the Trumbull upgrade are 365 Data Centers and Aphorio Carter, and First Selectman Vicki Tesoro has said the AI upgrade will not increase the facility's size, water use, electrical needs or noise. Residents remain uneasy because the property has substantial room for expansion, and Richard White of the Trumbull AI Data Center Watch group argued the site would run out of power long before it ran out of space. When the newspaper asked for the companies' letter of intent, a 365 Data Centers representative refused, calling the document confidential and non-binding. Residents who toured the facility with the executives said the meeting offered little reassurance without written commitments they could enforce. Sarah Beck, another resident, said she does not expect the corporations to keep their word without regulations in place.

Industry voices expect this kind of hybrid design to spread. Bill Kleyman, co-founder and CEO of the AI company Apolo.us, said he believes older facilities will need AI infrastructure to keep clients in fields such as higher education, research and finance. He expects that small data centers will keep handling tasks like email and photo storage while taking on more work. The residents' stated goal is a binding written guarantee that the Trumbull facility stays within its limits, so that the town becomes an example of how to keep a growing data center from harming its community. The article does not say whether any such guarantee will be made or when the upgrade will be complete.

Articles.Title: New England’s old buildings and old data centers could be upgraded to handle AI computing - WBUR

stories.Headline: Cudequest opposes AI data center; race uncontested
stories.Summary:
Montvale's Council President Theresa Cudequest is running unopposed for re-election to the Borough Council, alongside Councilman Douglas Arendacs, in the Nov. 3 election. Both are Republican incumbents seeking two seats as the borough weighs a decision over affordable housing and the possible development of a large artificial intelligence data center. Cudequest answered questions from the Pascack Press, while Arendacs did not respond to several requests for his positions. Her answers were the only public statement from either candidate on the matter.

The question centers on about 34 acres of the former KPMG office campus on Chestnut Ridge Road, where the borough and the Fair Share Housing Center disagree over how the site fits into Montvale's affordable housing obligations. The dispute is set for a hearing in Superior Court in Hackensack on Nov. 18. One option would allow a data center alongside 50 affordable housing units, while another would provide 250 residential units, including 50 affordable ones. Officials said the property is already zoned for data center use but distinguished conventional facilities from large AI computing sites, which can place heavier demands on electricity and cooling. A concept discussed for the site included a 322,822-square-foot AI data center, though no formal application has reached the Planning Board.

Cudequest said she opposes a large AI data center because of its potential strain on energy and water, while noting that owners should be able to develop land within existing rules. She also said she does not support overdevelopment to meet the state's affordable housing mandate, preferring to focus on the required number of affordable units and community benefits such as recreation facilities or a community center. Residents and environmental advocates have raised concerns at council meetings about electricity and water use, noise, and emissions from backup diesel generators. Cudequest named responsible development and community safety as her main priorities for another term.

Cudequest has served on the council twice, from 2010 through 2015 and again since December 2021, when she was appointed to fill an unexpired term. She was chosen as council president in January 2026. A 38-year resident who volunteered with the Tri-Boro Ambulance Corps for 21 years, she also works as a registered nurse at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital in New York City. The articles do not report what follows the Nov. 18 hearing or whether an application for the site will be filed.

Articles.Title: Cudequest opposes AI data center; race uncontested - Pascack Press & Northern Valley Press

AI's energy demand raises concerns about power grids and utility rates.

Those concerns are a top consideration for local communities weighing data center projects across the United States. stories.Headline: Column-streaming optical convolution with programmable MZIs processor
stories.Summary:
Researchers have published a paper describing a column-streaming optical convolution scheme that runs on a programmable processor built from Mach–Zehnder interferometers (MZIs). The work appeared in PhotoniX Synergy with a publication date of 5 October 2026, and it is an open-access research article. The authors map an N by N convolution kernel directly onto a single N by N MZI processor by transposing the kernel so that its weights match the column-by-column order of the input data. Two-dimensional convolution is then broken into a series of low-dimensional linear operations, and the outputs are recombined by backend shift-add accumulation.

The authors say the approach removes the need for a higher-dimensional N-squared by N-squared processor or for several N by N sub-processors working together. They tested it on a fabricated silicon photonic processor under different kernels, reporting root-mean-square errors below 0.061 compared with electrical reference results. They also built a hybrid optoelectronic convolutional neural network for MNIST handwritten digit classification, which reached an inference accuracy of 92 percent. According to the paper, both existing routes to MZI-based convolution add hardware scale, control difficulty and cost, which this scheme is meant to reduce for small kernels.

The paper is credited to its research authors, and the abstract presents the results as establishing a compact route to kernel convolution on programmable photonic processors. The article frames the work as a step toward integrated optical neural computing, though it does not describe any commercial deployment. The introduction places the research within a broader effort to ease the throughput, latency and energy demands that artificial intelligence models place on conventional electronic hardware. Beyond the reported experiments, the articles provided do not say what follow-up work the authors plan or how the scheme would scale to larger kernels in practice.

Articles.Title: Column-streaming optical convolution with programmable MZIs processor

stories.Headline: Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models
stories.Summary:
Cerebras, the AI chip company, published a technical post on October 25, 2026 explaining how it runs trillion-parameter frontier models across multiple wafer-scale chips. The post uses Kimi K3, an open source model with about 3 trillion parameters, as its worked example. Cerebras says its WSE-3T wafer carries 44 GB of on-chip memory, while models of this size need terabytes for their weights alone. The company says this approach can run multi-trillion-parameter models at 1,000 to 2,000-plus tokens per second.

The method rests on splitting the model across many wafers and keeping most of its weights in place on chip. The post assumes 4-bit weight quantization, an 8-bit KV cache and an average request size of 256k. Each model layer is about 16 GB, so a wafer can hold two linear-attention layers, which need no per-token cache, or one dense layer that leaves room for its KV cache. For Kimi K3, with 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers, Cerebras calculates a total of 59 wafers, which is 35 for the linear layers plus 24 for the dense layers. Wafers are linked over RDMA over Ethernet at roughly 2 microseconds per hop, so only activations pass between chips.

Cerebras credits the design to its pipeline approach, in which each wafer acts as one stage and many requests move through the stages at once. The post says the system does not run at an effective batch size of one because the pipeline stays full with different requests. The number of concurrent requests is set by how much on-chip memory remains for the KV cache, and the post says the right efficiency measure is total token throughput per unit of power. The post names Sarah Chieng as the author and thanks several colleagues for review. It also says the same method can extend to larger models by adding wafers.

Articles.Title: Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models

stories.Headline: An expert explains how AI can predict vulnerable areas before extreme weather strikes
stories.Summary:
An expert interview published by Yahoo Tech on October 25, 2026, describes how spatial AI can predict which specific parts of a city are likely to fail before extreme weather hits. The interview features Hantz Févry, CEO of Geolava, a technology lab that builds AI models for the physical world. Weather AI tools such as Google DeepMind's GraphCast, Huawei's Pangu-Weather and ECMWF's AIFS already forecast the atmosphere by learning patterns from decades of historical data, and agencies like NOAA and ECMWF use such systems to track large-scale events. Févry says spatial AI goes further by estimating what a given storm will do to a particular culvert, road or block.

According to the article, Geolava's platform, Terra, continuously observes roads, sidewalks, drainage and nearby vegetation, scores their condition, tracks how fast they are degrading and forecasts what will happen if current conditions continue. Févry says the system is built to work with incomplete records, relying mainly on aerial, satellite and street-level imagery, and that in Jacksonville the company checked and corrected a city's sidewalk inventory against what was on the ground. He says forecasts are reissued whenever new observations arrive so that errors get corrected, and that the tool supports engineers and city staff rather than replacing their decisions. The article also notes the company's work with the Florida Department of Transportation, where it says it forecast flood risk on road assets with about 87 percent accuracy, and that the department recently signed a multi-million-dollar, multi-year contract with Geolava.

Févry names the Florida Department of Transportation as the clearest example of the approach working, and he describes measuring success by forecast accuracy against outcomes, the lead time given to the department, reductions in emergency repairs and storm-related closures, and cost avoided per dollar spent. He acknowledges that no model is perfect and says the bigger risk is the current system, in which inspections often follow complaints and neighborhoods that do not call in problems can be missed. He also says the digital divide is a real concern and that Geolava and its public-sector partners must keep smaller and less-resourced communities from being last in line. Looking ahead to a hypothetical 2035 hurricane, he describes a city using such tools to pre-position crews and pumps at the most at-risk assets and to pick evacuation routes that are forecast to remain passable.

Articles.Title: An expert explains how AI can predict vulnerable areas before extreme weather strikes

stories.Headline: Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) Stock Looks Fully Valued Despite AI Hopes
stories.Summary:
