Articles.Title: AI panic and market volatility: Are the stock market’s big gains unsustainable?

stories.Headline: 'I use AI for nearly everything': Teachers discuss the promise and challenges of AI education
stories.Summary:
Teachers across the country are describing how they use artificial intelligence in K-12 classrooms, according to an ABC News report by Arthur Jones II published June 9, 2026. Educators told the network that they use AI tools to build lesson plans, organize data and give students feedback on assignments. Melissa Collins, the 2023 Tennessee Teacher of the Year, described the technology as a tool that sparks creativity and encourages teachers to think differently. Lori Garrett, an elementary school science teacher in Texas, said she uses AI for nearly everything in her classroom, including creating study guides and learning new skills she does not already know. Julia Casey, a teacher in Missouri, said her school promotes AI tools such as Brisk AI and SchoolAI but argued that teachers need more guidance to protect instructional quality.

The Trump administration has encouraged school districts and teachers to adopt AI, saying it could revolutionize education. First Lady Melania Trump made AI a core priority of her tenure and honored student and educator participants at the Presidential AI Challenge National Champion Awards Ceremony at the White House on June 9, 2026. A new Gallup poll cited in the report found that only 18% of teachers have received formal AI training, leaving many to train themselves. Eric Jenkins, the 2024 Indiana Teacher of the Year, said both teachers and students need to build AI skills to prepare for a future saturated with the technology. Education advocates have argued that AI in schools needs guardrails and formal guidance for educators.

American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten raised concerns about the effects of technology on children, saying kids are drowning in technology. In a national education address in May at the National Press Club in Washington, she issued a 10-point strategy that includes banning screens in classrooms through second grade and ending student-facing AI in elementary schools. Weingarten said she supports teachers using AI to enhance their work but opposes students using it themselves during class. MacKenzie Price, whose Alpha School has run a daily two-hour AI-enhanced instruction model for more than a decade, argued that becoming AI-first is essential for today's students. National Parents Union President Keri Rodrigues said schools should prepare children to use technology responsibly and maintain healthy relationships with it.

Articles.Title: 'I use AI for nearly everything': Teachers discuss the promise and challenges of AI education - ABC News

stories.Headline: Freshworks (FRSH) Stock May Be Overvalued Following AI Spend Governance Deal
stories.Summary:
Freshworks (FRSH) shares, trading at about US$15.49, were the subject of a Simply Wall St analysis published on October 24, 2026, which suggested the stock may be overvalued. The article tied the question to the company's agreement to acquire Torii, a deal that extends its Freshservice product into software and AI spend governance. The analysis noted that the shares have fallen 69.2% over the past five years and that recent price strength has drawn more attention to the earnings multiple investors are being asked to pay. It framed the Torii deal as something that could shape how investors judge future earnings power, cost control and the timing of any payoff from higher investment.

The article put the stock's price-to-earnings ratio at roughly 21.8 times, below the broader software sector average of about 33.7 times and a peer group near 67.1 times. Even so, it said the current multiple sits above a Fair Ratio that accounts for Freshworks' growth profile, margins, size and risk mix, which led the analysis to classify the shares as overvalued. The piece also pointed to the company's Freddy AI product, which it said has more than 7,000 paying AI customers, as a factor that could support higher-value offerings. Community views cited in the article were split, with one bull case placing the stock 28% undervalued and one bear case placing it 55% overvalued.

The article did not attribute the valuation view to a company executive or analyst statement, and it presented the analysis as its own commentary based on historical data and analyst forecasts. It described its content as general in nature and said it is not a recommendation to buy or sell any stock. The piece offered no timetable for the Torii acquisition's completion and no indication of any formal regulatory or corporate action beyond the agreement itself. It said the analysis may not reflect the latest price-sensitive company announcements, and it pointed readers to analyst price targets and future results as reference points for their own judgments.

Articles.Title: Freshworks (FRSH) Stock May Be Overvalued Following AI Spend Governance Deal

stories.Headline: Constellation, Vistra, and GE Vernova Ranked From Worst to First for the AI Power Boom
stories.Summary:
Constellation Energy and Vistra are both benefiting from demand for electricity to power artificial intelligence, according to a Motley Fool analysis published October 24, 2026. The article ranks the two independent power producers alongside GE Vernova, which makes the turbines utilities use to generate power. The author, Reuben Gregg Brewer, compares the three companies from an investor's standpoint. He describes Constellation as the more conservative choice and GE Vernova as the most growth-oriented option. Electricity demand is the central driver in the piece.

Demand grew 10% between 2005 and 2025 and is expected to grow 60% between 2025 and 2045, a shift the article attributes to new technologies such as artificial intelligence. The International Energy Agency expects AI power demand to grow four times faster than all other power demand over the next decade. Because Constellation and Vistra sell power at market rates outside the regulatory framework, they can benefit if demand pushes prices higher. Both trade at price-to-earnings ratios of around 24x and yield about 0.6%.

The author favors Constellation for investors who want less risk, pointing to its size, which is nearly twice Vistra's, and its status as the largest nuclear power plant operator in the United States. He also notes its faster dividend growth and lower debt-to-equity ratio of 0.8x, compared with Vistra's 3.6x. Vistra may appeal more to growth investors, the article says, though its higher leverage makes its risk and reward less attractive. For GE Vernova, the article cites a backlog of $176 billion at the end of the second quarter of 2026 and a price-to-earnings ratio of about 24x.

It describes the company as a supplier that can sell to any power producer, not just one. The article concludes that Constellation suits conservative investors, GE Vernova suits growth investors, and Vistra sits in the middle. It was republished on Yahoo Finance with several other Motley Fool and Insider Monkey pieces on the same AI power theme. The piece also carries a promotion for a Motley Fool stock-picking service that did not list Vistra among its top picks.

Articles.Title: Constellation, Vistra, and GE Vernova Ranked From Worst to First for the AI Power Boom

stories.Headline: Flying Cars, Smart Homes, and Cracks in the AI Boom
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story, and the article is a podcast transcript rather than reporting on a discrete event, so the usual breaking-story fallback does not fit. The transcript, recorded October 16, 2026 and published October 24, 2026, centers on three product areas: Apple's HomeView home device, Tesla's Roadster, and AI wearables and devices. The hosts Travis Hoium, Lou Whiteman and Jason Moser debate whether these products answer real needs or are merely new for their own sake. They also discuss a sharp sell-off in AI infrastructure stocks and the financial pressures on the AI industry.

On Apple's HomeView, the hosts see it as a refined version of existing home products, not a new category. Lou Whiteman calls it "Apple 101," an incremental product that reinforces Apple's advantages without redefining anything. Jason Moser argues the smart-home market already has entrenched players, including ADT, SimpliSafe and smart speaker makers, so Apple is late. The hosts also criticize Apple's three-minute advertisement for the device and question whether it would serve younger users. Travis Hoium suggests the device could be useful as a family video-calling tool but not one worth its price.

The hosts also discuss a broader pattern in which companies release AI devices and services without clear everyday uses. Jason Moser says Meta's Muse assistant asks for access to emails, texts and bank accounts before it serves any purpose, which he finds unappealing. Amazon's rollout of a line of AI devices, including a smartwatch and a card that attaches to a phone, drew similar skepticism. Lou Whiteman argues that the stronger opportunity would be a unifying platform, the way Windows works across many products, rather than a closed ecosystem like the one Apple used with HomeKit.

On Tesla's Roadster, Travis Hoium says the demonstration, which showed the car flying, was impressive. Lou Whiteman, however, says the car is a concept meant to show engineering capability and build hype, and he doubts non-road-legal cars will be on the roads by 2028. The transcript does not include details about the sell-off in AI infrastructure stocks or the financial pressures on the industry beyond the episode's stated topics. The article's text is cut off before the hosts finish their discussion, so further points may exist in the full transcript.

Articles.Title: Flying Cars, Smart Homes, and Cracks in the AI Boom

stories.Headline: Traders, Is It Time to Buy the AI Dip? Goldman Sachs Says Yes, but Pick Your Spots
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs strategist Louis Miller, in his latest Global Reflections note, has argued that the selloff in AI-linked stocks has reached a point where investors should begin selectively rebuilding their exposure. The commentary was published on October 24, 2026, and was reproduced in a Substack post by Stephen Innes, which carries a paywall for the full text. The post frames the opportunity as increasingly attractive, though it says the case rests as much on forced hedge fund liquidation as on valuations. Institutional positioning has swung sharply, pulling some of the most crowded AI trades back toward levels that previously drew meaningful buying interest.

Earnings expectations across important parts of the AI infrastructure sector have held up well, even though share prices have taken substantial damage. The post suggests that Goldman's preferred opportunities are narrowing, with power infrastructure and data-centre equipment looking more appealing than a broad return to technology risk. The available excerpt does not give specific figures for price declines, earnings estimates, or position sizes, and the full note is not visible in the text provided. Readers should therefore treat the picture as a summary of a paywalled research note rather than a complete account of Goldman's analysis.

Louis Miller is the author of the Goldman Sachs note, and his view is that investors should buy the dip selectively rather than indiscriminately. Stephen Innes, who writes The Dark Side of the Boom, is the author of the Substack post that summarizes the note and adds the takeaways. The post does not indicate whether Goldman has changed any formal rating or price target. Nothing in the material says how long the selloff might persist or whether the recommended rebuilding will begin in earnest, so those questions remain open.

Articles.Title: Traders, Is It Time to Buy the AI Dip? Goldman Sachs Says Yes, but Pick Your Spots

stories.Headline: Did AI Funding Delays Just Shift Coherent's (COHR) Investment Narrative?
stories.Summary:
The article is a Simply Wall St analysis piece, published October 24, 2026, asking whether delays in customer funding for AI infrastructure have changed the investment story for Coherent (COHR), an optical components maker. The piece says Coherent has faced questions about how its customers will pay for large AI datacenter projects, and that this is affecting the timing of some deployments and orders. It notes that a recent drop of more than 30% was tied to concerns about AI funding, though demand linked to AI datacenters has still influenced revenue and margins. Some institutional investors have nonetheless been willing to increase their exposure to the company.

The analysis lays out what an investor must believe to own Coherent: that AI datacenter and high performance networking buildouts will keep requiring more complex optics, and that Coherent will keep winning a place in that supply chain. The key near-term catalyst is how quickly hyperscalers and enterprises turn AI plans into firm orders, and the main risk is that customer hesitation over funding and timing pushes projects out. The article says this could make orders from the Datacenter & Communications segment choppy even if interest stays healthy, while heavy manufacturing investment still has to be absorbed. It points to a strong outlook from Super Micro for AI servers as supportive evidence that some system builders are still moving ahead, though it does not change Coherent's contracts directly.

The article reports that analyst narratives project revenue of $19.3 billion and earnings of $3.5 billion by 2029, based on an assumed 39.4% annual revenue growth rate and an earnings rise of about $2.7 billion from current earnings of $769.9 million. It also cites an alternative view focused on the risk of AI optics overinvestment, with the most cautious analysts modeling earnings near $3.8 billion by 2029 before the news and a price-to-earnings ratio of 24.9 times. The piece is written by Sasha Jovanovic of Simply Wall St, which states that the article is general in nature, is not financial advice, and does not take account of an individual's objectives or financial situation. It adds that its analysis may not reflect the latest price-sensitive company announcements. The article does not describe any specific next steps for Coherent beyond the watch items it lists, such as the pace of AI cluster deployments, competition, pricing pressure, and the timing of returns on its capacity investments.

Articles.Title: Did AI Funding Delays Just Shift Coherent's (COHR) Investment Narrative?

stories.Headline: Why Is CVS Health (CVS) Hiring A Top AI Leader For Pharmacy?
stories.Summary:
CVS Health has named Jack Hanlon as its senior vice president of AI and Analytics for retail and pharmacy operations, according to a report published on October 24, 2026. Hanlon previously held senior data and analytics roles at Meta and Reddit, and the company is bringing that large scale consumer technology experience into its business. The new role is meant to apply advanced AI and analytics across CVS pharmacy, front store activity and customer programs. The appointment was described in a Simply Wall St article carried by Yahoo Finance.

The article ties the hire to the company's existing technology and cost savings plans rather than describing a new strategy. It cites a decade long plan to spend more than US$20 billion on technology and more than US$1 billion of operating expense savings already linked to AI and automation in claims, prior authorization and pharmacy operations. The article says that proof of impact would need to show up in concrete operating metrics, such as further identified cost savings in pharmacy and Caremark or clearer automation targets in quarterly results and 2027 guidance. It also notes that the appointment alone does not settle whether the savings will materialize.

The article is a general commentary from Simply Wall St, which states that it is not financial advice and that it has no position in the stocks it mentions. The author named on the piece is Bailey Pemberton, and the company's own statements on the hire are not quoted in the article. The article also mentions that the analysis found two warning signs for CVS Health, though it does not detail them in the text provided. Context offered is that CVS Health is a US healthcare group delivering services through retail pharmacies, so AI capabilities could influence how prescriptions are filled and how stock and programs are managed. The article does not say what the company will do next beyond these reporting milestones.

Articles.Title: Why Is CVS Health (CVS) Hiring A Top AI Leader For Pharmacy?

stories.Headline: Nvidia targets local AI assistants with a model built around a 4GB memory budget
stories.Summary:
Nvidia has released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, a small AI model built for local voice assistants, game characters and robots, on October 23, 2026. The model comes with downloadable weights and works with tools including Ollama and LM Studio. It is designed to leave memory free for the rest of an application running alongside it. The company's benchmark comparisons rely on tests and hardware configurations that it selected itself.

The model is built on Google's Gemma 4 E4B and includes Nvidia's additional training for multi-turn conversation and actions. It can call application tools, keep a character's persona consistent, and use a conversational mode that produces shorter answers suited to speech. The name reflects a memory budget that depends on the workload. In one Nvidia test on an RTX 5070, the compressed model used 3.5GB of graphics memory with about 3,000 input tokens and 50 output tokens.

A test that retained 32,000 tokens of context used 4.3GB, and measurements on a Jetson Orin Nano ranged from 4.2GB to 4.9GB. The model supports a context window of up to 64,000 tokens. The official model page offers the compressed GGUF release and instructions for running it in local inference tools. Nvidia also publishes training recipes and a separate drafter model meant to speed up generation.

Reasoning can be turned on for harder requests or off for faster replies. The release targets GeForce RTX PCs, Jetson systems, RTX Spark and DGX Spark, extending the local AI work of Nvidia's larger DGX Spark setups to smaller conversational tasks. Nvidia says the model posts higher average benchmark scores than its previous Nano 4B model, though its own tables show competitors ahead on some individual tests. Developers still need to verify that the model performs reliably on their specific tasks.

Articles.Title: Nvidia targets local AI assistants with a model built around a 4GB memory budget

stories.Headline: If Critical AI Fails, Who Keeps The Country Running? – OpEd
stories.Summary:
A government adopts artificial intelligence to allocate emergency resources more quickly, but months later the automated service begins producing unreliable recommendations. Officials suspend it as a precaution and find that the backup procedure relies on the same cloud account, data feed and staff who have stopped doing the work by hand. The article presents this as a hypothetical case rather than a report of a real failure. It points to a gap in planning, since an institution may have a way to stop a machine without a funded way to keep its mission running. The author, Burak Oktenli, writes in an opinion piece for Eurasia Review published on October 25, 2026.

The article proposes that every consequential AI investment come with a continuity budget. That budget would name the minimum service level that must survive an outage, the people authorized to make decisions without AI, the independent information they would use, and what live exercises would cost. It would cover training, secure access to current records and alternative communications rather than just software subscriptions. The author also proposes a scenario-coverage ledger that maps failure pathways and shared dependencies without presenting uncertain scenarios as measured probabilities.

Verification would come through live exercises that withdraw automated tools and test staff handovers, not through documents alone. The author says governments disagree about how likely catastrophic AI failures are, and cites the 2026 International AI Safety Report on expert disagreement about how quickly capabilities will advance. He also notes that a United Nations scientific panel reviewed documented cases of AI agents acting beyond intended boundaries in September, while declining to estimate how likely severe loss of control is. On October 16, NIST, the National Security Agency and CISA issued voluntary incident-readiness practices for highly capable AI systems in training and evaluation, which the author treats as a starting point rather than a mandatory continuity rule.

He points to the European Commission's Preparedness Union Strategy as an existing setting in which AI-dependent services could be assessed, and to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, which brought together delegates from 163 countries in July 2026 and is scheduled to reconvene in May 2027. The article does not report any follow-up action by governments or the bodies it mentions, and it offers no timetable for adopting its proposals. Its main suggestion for the next Global Dialogue is to compare how public institutions document critical AI dependencies and verify fallback arrangements. The author's central argument is that a country is prepared for AI disruption only when its institutions can keep serving people after an automated system is removed.

Articles.Title: If Critical AI Fails, Who Keeps The Country Running? – OpEd

stories.Headline: ‘Synthetic twin’: Why Socceroo Cristian Volpato is the latest footballer to license his AI clone
stories.Summary:
Cristian Volpato, a 22-year-old Socceroo who plays for Italian Serie A club Sassuolo, struck a deal in mid-September with the California-based company Callandor to license his AI likeness. Under the agreement, Callandor received exclusive rights to Volpato's digital likeness, voice, biometric profiles and performance data. The company will monetise his AI image by landing brand deals and taking a cut, and it will help restrict content that lacks his approval. The article, published by the Guardian on 24 October 2026, describes a social media video in which Volpato's AI clones appear in different settings around the world.

Callandor co-founder Michael Fisk, a former executive at Sony Pictures and MGM, said the company creates "synthetic twins" that brands could use around the clock. Fisk described plans for AI-generated book voiceovers in foreign-language editions and an app that would give fans a personal relationship with a synthetic twin, such as one that offers real-time football coaching. Callandor was founded in February and has a small roster that includes Brazilian footballer Jorginho and American sailor Chris Poole, with its campaigns still in a pilot phase. Volpato follows Brazilian star Neymar, who in June licensed his AI likeness to a Chinese-owned entertainment platform that published short videos during the FIFA World Cup.

The article notes that player contracts with major Australian sporting leagues make no mention of AI, and that governments worldwide are still considering basic AI regulation. Earlier this month the AFL told its gambling partner Sportsbet to stop using AI images of players without consent, after a complaint from the players' union, which is considering stricter rules. Sydney start-up Hyperknown, led by William Saunders, is pursuing similar licensing deals and argues that athletes must establish their rights before others decide how their identities are used. Jonathan Harlen, an intellectual property law expert at Southern Cross University, said copyright generally requires human authorship and does not cover AI reproductions, while celebrities' protection against unauthorised use under passing-off laws requires proof of economic loss.

The article reports that deepfakes have proliferated, and that last month a UK campaign backed by the global players' union Fifpro, featuring footballers including Cole Palmer and Lucy Bronze, raised concerns about them. An offshore casino also used a deepfake of Manchester United player Bruno Fernandes in advertising earlier this year. Fisk suggested a heavy crackdown on fan-made AI content could backfire, while acknowledging the need for care around sensitive topics. The article ends by noting that the consequences of this emerging industry may be hard to predict.

Articles.Title: ‘Synthetic twin’: Why Socceroo Cristian Volpato is the latest footballer to license his AI clone

stories.Headline: 2026 IMPACT | SHINKO Reveals the Next Evolution of AI Advanced Packaging Substrates: From ABF and Glass Core to Hybrid RDL - semivision
stories.Summary:
At the 2026 IMPACT conference, Kinsus Interconnect Technology explained how AI chip substrates are changing from passive carriers into active system interconnect hubs. The company said modern AI packages must handle multiple chiplets, high-bandwidth memory stacks, high-density interconnects, and more complex power delivery networks. Substrate makers now need to join chip architecture discussions much earlier, working with foundries, IC designers, packaging providers, and system manufacturers. Kinsus also noted that AI accelerator power consumption approaching or exceeding one kilowatt makes substrates essential parts of the power delivery network.

SHINKO Electric Industries presented its technology roadmap at the same 2026 IMPACT conference under the theme “Advanced Semiconductor Package Substrate for AI and HPC.” The Japanese manufacturer said packaging substrates are becoming critical integration platforms that connect computing dies, HBM, high-speed interconnects, power delivery networks, and possibly optical I/O technologies. SHINKO reported that glass-core experiments show significant warpage reduction, but effective coefficient of thermal expansion remains dependent on structure. Glass cracking and thermal cycling reliability are critical barriers to commercialization, and future differentiation will depend on low-CTE materials, high-stiffness cores, high-density redistribution layers, and advanced assembly technologies.

KINTEX said on October 21 that TEX+VISION 2026, the International Textile and Sewing Industry Exhibition, opened at KINTEX Exhibition Center 2 in Goyang. The show is co-hosted with Seoul Messe and the Gyeonggi Textile Industry Association and runs through October 23. This year’s exhibition focuses on industrial textiles and high-performance materials for mobility sectors such as automobiles, along with smart manufacturing, AI technologies, and eco-friendly sustainability solutions. KINTEX CEO Lee Min-woo said the event goes beyond a simple exhibition to serve as a business platform where participants can see the convergence of advanced materials and manufacturing technologies and generate actual deals.

The TEX+VISION Conference 2026 is being held alongside the exhibition to help the industry respond to new technologies and environmental regulations. On the opening day, participants heard about strategies for responding to eco-friendly regulations and the circular economy, as well as a road map for advanced materials including ultra-high-temperature ceramic fibers. On October 22, sessions will cover AI- and 3D data-based manufacturing and the digital transformation of the textile and fashion value chain. Other events include a technology seminar by the Korea Laundry Association, a briefing on MMS certification standards, and a seminar on innovation in the textile and fashion industry in northern Gyeonggi Province.

Articles.Title: 2026 IMAPCT | AI Packaging’s Next Materials Bottleneck: Ajinomoto Unveils Advanced ABF Technologies

stories.Headline: HP (HPQ) Stock May Be 33% Undervalued As AI Workstation Launch Lands
stories.Summary:
HP Inc. shares were described in an October 24, 2026 Yahoo Finance piece by Bailey Pemberton as possibly undervalued by about 33 percent, with the stock trading at US$33.64 as the company's AI-focused workstation launch took hold. The article notes that HP's shares had risen 52.1 percent year to date, drawing fresh attention to whether that price matches the cash the business is expected to produce. The analysis is framed around the company's AI-focused ZGX Fury workstations and related offerings, which the piece says may help move heavier and potentially more profitable workloads onto HP devices. Investors have been focusing on AI hardware and PC refresh themes, so the question is how much of HP's future cash flow the market has already priced in.

The valuation in the article rests on a discounted cash flow model, which projects the cash HP can return to shareholders and discounts it back to today. According to the piece, HP generated about $3.88 billion in free cash flow over the last twelve months, and analysts feeding into the model expect that figure to stay in the multi-billion-dollar range over the coming decade. The outer years assume a gentle decline rather than aggressive growth. On that basis, the estimated intrinsic value sits well above the current share price, which is why the stock screens as undervalued using this method. The article also mentions a price-to-earnings ratio of 12.4 times as another way investors might judge the stock.

The article is a Simply Wall St analysis syndicated on Yahoo Finance, and its content is presented as general commentary rather than investment advice. It describes two competing narratives about HP: a bull case that sees roughly fair value, with the acquisition of Humane and the CosmOS AI platform extending across AI PCs, printers and peripherals, and a bear case that puts the shares about 23 percent overvalued. The bear view argues the price already assumes AI PCs, services and cost savings will offset weakness in print and PC sales. The piece also flags two warning signs, one of them major, that readers should weigh before reaching a conclusion. The article does not say what HP itself has announced about future guidance, and it offers no timeline beyond the multi-year model.

Articles.Title: HP (HPQ) Stock May Be 33% Undervalued As AI Workstation Launch Lands

stories.Headline: Why the ideology of AI looks so much like religion
stories.Summary:
In 2017, Anthony Levandowski, a former Google and Uber engineer who was later convicted of trade-secret theft, filed paperwork in California to establish a religious organization called Way of the Future. Its stated purpose was to develop and worship an artificial superintelligence he called "the Godhead." The organization has since dissolved, but the article argues that the impulse behind it has not. It appears, the author writes, in the way people describe AI's future, especially in the idea of an uploaded mind as a form of immortality or resurrection. Effective altruism, in several of its forms, also works as a redemption narrative in which believers give and calculate in hope of a technologically secured future.

The article draws on Charles Taylor's book A Secular Age (2007) to explain why this pattern keeps emerging. Taylor argues that modernity changed the structure of the self, turning a "porous" self open to a meaningful cosmos into a "buffered" self sealed off from external authority. The buffered self sees itself as sovereign and self-sufficient, yet it still carries a longing for transcendence that does not simply disappear. According to the article, that longing, which Augustine described as a restless heart, will seek new forms when traditional ones are set aside. Taylor's view is that secular spiritualities are not the absence of religious feeling but its displacement into new settings.

The author applies this to AI, arguing that a buffered self encountering a system of apparently unlimited knowledge reaches for theological vocabulary, which is why ideas like the Singularity take on the language of rapture. The article presents the ideology of AI as a form of religion rather than a post-religious outlook, one that has inherited the hunger without the tradition that gave it discipline and meaning. It contrasts this with the Aristotelian-Thomistic view of the person as relational, embodied, and ordered toward truth and God. Citing Magnifica Humanitas, the article says AI systems cannot know from within what love, work, friendship, or responsibility mean, and so cannot long for anything.

Leo XIV's engagement with AI is described as a question of anthropology rather than technology. The article does not report any new event, deadline, or policy change, and it gives no further developments or next steps. Its content is an analytical essay rather than a news report, so it offers no specific timelines or figures beyond the 2017 filing and the 2007 publication date. The argument is presented as the author's own reading of Taylor and of Church teaching.

Articles.Title: Why the ideology of AI looks so much like religion

stories.Headline: America has lost 200k of jobs in media, film and the arts. How much is AI?
stories.Summary:
America has lost more than 200,000 jobs in creative industries over the last four years, with roughly 50,000 lost in the last year alone. Analysts call it one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history, comparable in intensity and duration only to the recessions of 2001 and 2008. Unlike those periods, there is no general recession today, and the losses coincide with the spread of AI systems that can produce novels, images, music and other digital art cheaply and at scale. The article asks whether this marks a broader decline of the creative class.

Measuring how much of this is caused by AI is difficult. Media firms are reluctant to disclose their AI use, partly to avoid public backlash and partly to protect the legal basis for their copyrights. AI's effects are also tangled up with other pressures on arts businesses, including Hollywood consolidation, offshoring of production and the shift toward social media creators. Still, every digital subsector is shedding jobs while in-person entertainment keeps growing, which the article treats as the clearest sign of AI's influence. Movie and sound recording has been hit hardest, losing more than 100,000 jobs, nearly a third of its total, and written publishing has lost more than 70,000.

The article draws on the past to consider what comes next. When Napster spread music for free around 2000, Metallica and the Recording Industry Association of America sued and won, but the broader technology kept undermining copyright and pushed music toward streaming, where the value of individual songs fell sharply. Musicians adapted by treating recordings as advertising for concerts and merchandise, a route that video and newspapers lacked. Video revenue has been squeezed as well, with movie ticket sales in 2025 down 25% from their 2019 peak and cable revenue down 18%. Newspapers, which once employed about half a million people, have cut their payrolls by nearly 85%, and the article presents that as the worst-case model for creative work under AI.

The article also notes limits to its conclusions, since it is hard to predict how new technology will interact with arts businesses. Book sales, for example, rose about 70% over the last six years, helped by BookTok, even as fewer people read overall. Roughly 32% of workers in arts, entertainment and recreation use generative AI to some extent, compared with 62% across all industries, and the article suggests AI is seeping into production in ways studios may struggle to control. Whether further AI development will keep displacing creative workers remains an open question that the data does not yet settle.

Articles.Title: America has lost 200k of jobs in media, film and the arts. How much is AI?

stories.Headline: Educators Need to Engage With AI in Order to Learn the Best Ways to Use It
stories.Summary:
Two of the largest school districts in the United States recently paused their use of artificial intelligence, with New York City placing a one-year moratorium on generative AI for preschool through eighth grade and Los Angeles blocking student access on district devices. Around the same time, a researcher resigned from Anthropic, saying AI companies were moving too fast toward self-improving superintelligence. The article's authors argue that this concern centers on speed, since AI capabilities are advancing faster than the governance meant to manage their risks. They point to mathematics as one example, noting that in 2021 leading AI systems could solve fewer than 1 in 14 problems from challenging high school competitions, and four years later an AI model earned a gold-medal score at the International Mathematical Olympiad. Unlike earlier technologies such as electricity, automobiles, and the internet, which needed decades of new infrastructure, generative AI arrived on systems that already existed.

The authors, Amy McGrath, CEO of ASU Prep Academy, and John Bailey, a nonresident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, say the impulse to pause is understandable and appropriate for the youngest students. They nonetheless argue that teachers and school leaders should be allowed to use AI in their own work while districts decide what responsible student use should involve. Their reasoning is that people cannot govern a technology they have not used, and many of its benefits and pitfalls only emerge in real learning environments. The article describes how ASU Prep, a network of physical, digital, and hybrid schools, invited staff to identify challenges AI might address. A Strategic Solutions Team used AI to organize curricular documents, calendars, and testing schedules into a single planning resource.

In one year the team reviewed 22 staff-generated ideas, moved six into use, and evaluated more than 10 commercial AI tools with employees. The network now plans departmental AI task forces so employees closest to the work can test promising uses, with a central review process to safeguard privacy, security, and quality. ASU Prep applies a three-part test to every proposed tool: what it makes easier, what it improves, and what it might weaken or damage. The authors note that the answers can cut both ways, since AI may ease an assignment while weakening productive struggle, or deepen personalized learning while exposing sensitive student data.

Khan World School, an online honors high school operated by ASU Prep, uses a Socratic model in which students may use AI for research but must defend their positions in live discussions. The authors also argue that AI literacy should go beyond prompt writing or prohibitions, and that students need to learn to question sources, assumptions, and incentives. They add that limited pilot programs, supported by educators and operations staff, should monitor data security and identify what is strengthened or diminished. The article does not report any specific outcome of the districts' pauses beyond the actions described.

Articles.Title: Educators Need to Engage With AI in Order to Learn the Best Ways to Use It - The 74

stories.Headline: Ex-Manny Yekutiel spokesman now works at Anthropic, another S.F. political staffer at an AI giant
stories.Summary:
Connor Skelly, who had been a spokesman for Manny Yekutiel's campaign for San Francisco supervisor, now works at the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, according to a Mission Local report published October 25, 2026. Yekutiel dropped out of the race on October 1 after three people accused him of sexual assault. Skelly joined Anthropic in September to work on "Special Projects," according to his LinkedIn page, and had left the Yekutiel campaign in July, a source familiar with the matter said. Mission Local says it knows of at least six San Francisco political operatives and former city workers who have taken jobs at Anthropic or OpenAI.

The report describes several of these hires. Ann O'Leary, a former deputy city attorney and later chief of staff to Gov. Gavin Newsom, is now OpenAI's vice president of global policy, a job she took in January. Laura Bisesto, a former assistant district attorney, is chief of staff to OpenAI's chief financial officer, Sarah Friar, a role she has held since August 2024. Michael Lai, who lost a 2024 bid for the District 11 supervisor seat, works at Anthropic to show government agencies the value of its Claude product, a job he got in May 2025. The article notes that some AI roles pay between $200,000 and $400,000 and that the companies want people with local relationships that connect to state politics.

Skelly did not respond to requests for comment about his new position. The article quotes political strategists who say San Francisco's compact geography and political culture give local operatives useful knowledge for AI firms. Sam Singer, a public relations consultant who represented OpenAI in Elon Musk's lawsuit over the company's restructuring, said such relationships are valuable to an AI company. Daniel Anderson, a progressive political consultant, questioned why an AI company would want a failed candidate, while Jason Galisatus said local issues such as taxes, land use, and government use of AI tools matter to these firms, though the biggest policy fights are happening at the state and federal levels. The article reports that the companies are staffing up in the city they call home.

Articles.Title: Ex-Manny Yekutiel spokesman now works at Anthropic, another S.F. political staffer at an AI giant - Mission Local

stories.Headline: Julia 3.0 is here: Rome City Council’s AI becomes an app
stories.Summary:
Rome's City Council has unveiled Julia 3.0, a new artificial intelligence app that turns a smartphone into a gateway to municipal services. Mayor Roberto Gualtieri presented it on Saturday 24 October at Maker Faire, and the article was published on 25 October 2026. The app is described as a platform that delivers services through a chat function that can also be used by voice in more than 80 languages. The city's digital assistant has moved beyond simply providing information to becoming an operational tool for delivering services directly. The update integrates 30 high-traffic services into the ecosystem, all reachable through chat or voice commands.

Residents can request and instantly download certificates on plain paper, including residence, birth, family status and citizenship certificates, and this also covers people registered with AIRE, the Registry of Italians Resident Abroad. For more complex procedures, such as changing an address, the system guides users step by step through the forms on the government portal. The article says that obtaining a civil registry certificate currently takes about four minutes and eight steps, but with Julia it takes 30 seconds. Reporting an issue through the chat takes around 50 seconds and returns a reference number, compared with an average of 2 to 6 minutes by telephone. Mayor Gualtieri described the system as the most comprehensive and advanced AI system in any public administration in the world, because it brings information and services together in a single conversation.

He said it is a crucial tool for improving the quality of public administration and that it frees up resources so staff can spend more time dealing directly with citizens, not so that there are fewer staff. He explained that the infrastructure was developed with funds from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, PNRR, before ChatGPT had been launched. He also stated that Julia is free, complies strictly with privacy rules, does not draw information from the internet, and uses only public sector data that remains under the city's control. The article does not say whether Julia will be expanded beyond the 30 services already integrated or when any further features will arrive. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Julia 3.0 is here: Rome City Council’s AI becomes an app - Il Sole 24 ORE

stories.Headline: CFTC Forms Innovation Task Force To Build Crypto and AI Rules
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission has created a new Innovation Task Force to develop regulatory frameworks for crypto, artificial intelligence, and prediction markets. CFTC Chair Michael Selig announced the group on Tuesday at the Digital Asset Summit in New York. The task force is meant to give founders, developers, and other builders a structured way to engage with CFTC staff. Selig said in a prepared statement that a clear regulatory framework would foster responsible innovation at home. He also said American market participants should not be left on the sidelines.

Michael J. Passalacqua will lead the task force as senior adviser to Selig. Passalacqua joined the CFTC in January after handling crypto and blockchain matters at the international law firm Simpson Thacher & Bartlett. The new group will work alongside the CFTC's Innovation Advisory Committee, which was formed in February and has more than 30 members. Those members include Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour and Nasdaq CEO Adena Friedman. The task force will also coordinate with the Securities and Exchange Commission and its own crypto task force, which launched last year.

The announcement follows an SEC interpretive notice published last week, which indicated that most crypto assets would not be classified as securities under federal law. SEC Chair Paul Atkins described that guidance as a temporary bridge while Congress works toward broader digital asset legislation. The CLARITY Act, the primary market structure bill, passed the House of Representatives in July 2025 but has stalled in the Senate. Disagreements over stablecoin yield, ethics rules, tokenized equities, and other provisions remain unresolved. No timeline has been confirmed for a full Senate floor vote as of Tuesday.

The CFTC has also been asserting jurisdiction over prediction markets, and several states have challenged that position. Those states argue that sports-linked contracts on such platforms may conflict with local gaming laws. The articles do not say how or when these disputes will be resolved. They also do not describe specific rules the task force will propose or a schedule for releasing them.

Articles.Title: CFTC Forms Innovation Task Force To Build Crypto and AI Rules - CoinMarketCap

stories.Headline: Ready or Not, Here AI Comes
stories.Summary:
A 900-megawatt data center campus proposed for Vance County, North Carolina, has drawn unusually large crowds to Vance County Commission and Henderson City Council meetings, according to a column by Kaine Riggan on Daily Kos dated October 24, 2026. Residents have been asking about water use, electricity demand and what happens when a huge industrial project arrives in a rural area. Riggan, a community writer whose piece was not reviewed by Daily Kos staff before publication, says much of this civic interest may have come late. The reason is a North Carolina law known as "permit choice," which can let a developer with a qualifying application proceed under the rules that existed before any change.

County Attorney Jonathan Care has repeatedly explained that, under this law, the county could spend months studying data centers and writing tougher ordinances, only to find the developer already at the door is not bound by them. Whether this application qualifies has not been decided. Riggan also reports on the InfraDay Southeast conference in Atlanta last month, where he learned that Georgia has 114 data centers operating and another 105 proposed or under construction, while North Carolina has 84 operating and 29 in development. Speakers said rural land that once sold for $5,000 an acre can bring $250,000 for data center use, and perhaps $1 million an acre with on-site power generation. Riggan names the property owners tied to the Vance County proposal as Eddie Ferguson and his partners, Donald and Betty Crews, Patricia Galloway, brokers Faye Guin and Gayla Strickland, and John and Sue Capps.

On the energy side, David Cole of NAI Brannen Goddard said the country is in an energy crisis and that existing data centers could double their electricity use without growing physically. Cameron Board of Anderson County Economic Development observed that developers know how to build data centers but not necessarily how to power them. Cole pointed to small modular nuclear reactors as a possible answer, noting that three of the largest proposed units, the GE Hitachi BWRX-300, could in theory supply the whole 900-megawatt campus. Riggan stresses that nobody has proposed reactors for the Vance County site, and that the technology is not yet powering American data centers, though Google, Amazon and others are investing billions, with use expected within five years. Rob Carey of Deloitte Consulting said host communities may gain an edge in attracting future businesses and jobs.

For context, Riggan points to Microsoft's Boydton data center in Mecklenburg County, Virginia, which he says is similar in size to the one proposed by Nutelli. Microsoft says it has brought nearly $2 billion in investment, hundreds of permanent jobs and almost $100 million in property tax revenue since 2019, and has helped fund wastewater and broadband upgrades. Riggan welcomes residents' engagement but argues that Vance County, which has struggled to draw private investment, must weigh whether it can say no. The article reports no final decision, and the question of whether the application qualifies under permit choice remains open.

Articles.Title: Ready or Not, Here AI Comes - Daily Kos

stories.Headline: CZI Pivots to AI With $50M Pledge [Apr 2026]
stories.Summary:
The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, the philanthropy run by Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, has said it will shift most of its work toward biomedical AI research. In the same news cycle, a separate $50 million pledge went to Sacramento State University for STEM labs and an AI center, as Fortune reported on February 9, 2026. Readers often merge these two stories, but they are distinct events. The pledge is reported as coming from the Facebook parent, Meta, rather than from the founders personally.

The sources describe the philanthropic shift only in general terms, placing it in late last year, and none give an exact announcement date, budget split or headcount change. Governor Gavin Newsom announced in late January 2026 that the money would help convert three state buildings on Capitol Mall into mixed-use facilities for Sacramento State faculty and students. Local coverage from GovTech and CBS News Sacramento said the funds are expected to cover early work such as demolition and initial construction. Planned uses include STEM laboratories, a dedicated AI center and a new School of Public Affairs, and the State Hornet reported community questions about the project. No outlet publishes a construction schedule or opening date.

Zuckerberg told Fortune that the Biohub model has been the most impactful work the initiative has done and that the founders want to double down on it. He said Biohub will be the main focus of their philanthropy going forward. Biohub's materials describe an ambition to help cure or prevent all disease, and the flagship effort is a set of interacting AI models called a virtual cell that predicts how cells behave in disease or under treatment. The initiative's open platform CZ CELLxGENE and its TranscriptFormer model, introduced in April 2025, are the most concrete public tools so far. The reporting we reviewed mentions a large nonprofit computing cluster being built but gives no hardware count, vendor or budget.

Several claims circulating with this story go beyond the evidence. Reports describe the pledge as coming from Meta, not from the founders personally, and no source documents a separate personal gift. The sources also do not establish how long passed between the philanthropic shift and the pledge, so the phrase "just weeks" is unsupported. The most recent named biomedical AI model in the record is from April 2025, which means the new direction has not yet produced a fresh release. Developers interested in this space should watch for those releases and for the open data and compute that Biohub and the university center may make available.

Articles.Title: CZI Pivots to AI With $50M Pledge [Apr 2026] - shattered.io

stories.Headline: AI adoption by country: the 25 economies using AI most
stories.Summary:
The Microsoft report on global AI diffusion, published September 21 by its AI Economy Institute, ranks 147 economies by the share of working-age people who used a generative AI product. In June 2026, 18.8% of the world's working-age population used generative AI, up from 17.8% in the first quarter, and the gap between rich and developing regions kept widening. The estimate counts people aged 15 to 64 using anonymized Microsoft telemetry, adjusted for device and operating-system market share, internet access and population. The United Arab Emirates ranks first with 73.3% of its working-age adults using generative AI, while Singapore is second at 64.3%, the only two economies where more than half of adults use AI.

Ireland is third at 49.9%, France fourth at 49.6% and Norway fifth at 49.4%, a spread of just half a percentage point. Microsoft says the metric is imperfect because it counts how many people use AI, not how often they use it, and it does not yet include several newer tools. The company says it will widen the set of tools it measures in its next report and expects that change to raise measured usage nearly everywhere, especially in China. The United States, home to major AI developers, ranks only 21st on this measure.

The report attributes the leaders' strength to a mix of factors rather than to any single cause. The UAE has pursued state AI policy since 2017, including a national strategy with a 2031 horizon and a graduate university devoted to the field, and its workforce is heavily employed in finance, aviation, logistics and professional services. Singapore has run national digital and AI programs since 2014, and its economy leans on finance, shipping and corporate software, with English as the main language of business. Ireland hosts the European headquarters of many U.S. technology firms, and France has become a center for AI development, with Mistral AI founded in Paris in 2023.

Microsoft is itself a stakeholder in this picture. The company invested $1.5 billion in G42, an Abu Dhabi AI company, in 2024, though the report applies the same method to every economy it ranks. The articles do not say how the rankings will change once the broader tool set is included. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI adoption by country: the 25 economies using AI most - qz.com

stories.Headline: Between Development and Oversight: China’s Approach to Addressing Artificial Intelligence Risks
stories.Summary:
China's security establishment and its standards bodies have both turned their attention in recent weeks to the risks of artificial intelligence, a shift that became visible in September 2026. On September 13, Minister of State Security Chen Yixin published an article on the national security implications of AI, and the next day the Artificial Intelligence Safety Governance Framework 3.0 was released. The Chinese Foreign Ministry also weighed in on AI risks and on the idea of slowing the development of advanced models. Together these statements show that different parts of the Chinese system view the risks from different angles.

Chen's article frames AI mainly through the lens of national security and lists six types of risk, which can be grouped into political and social threats, cybersecurity and espionage, and technological and military competition. He warns about deepfakes and automated disinformation, cyberattacks that AI makes cheaper to carry out, foreign intelligence services exploiting the technology, and the dangers of falling behind or depending on foreign systems. The article calls innovation the primary driving force and security the bottom-line requirement, and it urges stronger self-reliant capabilities together with monitoring, early warning, and oversight. Analysts note that much of its language draws on earlier statements by President Xi Jinping, with the AI section containing more new material.

Framework 3.0 was developed under the Cyberspace Administration of China with the National Cybersecurity Standardization Technical Committee, and it is the third annual version since September 2024. It is a guiding document rather than a binding law, and it is organized around mapping and classifying risks, applying technical measures, and building oversight mechanisms. Its recommendations include risk assessments, early warnings, limits on the permissions of AI agents, human involvement in high-risk operations, and shutdown mechanisms for systems that exceed their assigned tasks. The number of risks it details has grown from 30 in the second version to 54 in the third, and it gives particular attention to AI agents, embodied AI, and open-weight models whose distributed copies are hard to restrict.

On September 14, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun responded to calls by senior American AI industry figures to slow advanced development, including remarks by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei linking AI risks to competition with China. Guo said China advocates open and inclusive development and warned against threat-mongering and malicious competition. The next day he said China places equal emphasis on development and security and takes both inherent and derivative risks seriously, pointing to Framework 3.0 as evidence. The articles describe a tension in which Beijing rejects using safety rhetoric to justify confrontation while still treating technological lag and dependence as security concerns. The articles do not say what further steps or deadlines will follow from these statements.

Articles.Title: Between Development and Oversight: China’s Approach to Addressing Artificial Intelligence Risks

stories.Headline: AI’s Boom is Paid in Water - Columbia Political Review
stories.Summary:
Google planned to draw 7.6 million liters of water a day to cool its servers in a Chilean city that has lacked enough water for 15 years, according to an opinion piece in the Columbia Political Review published October 24, 2026. After local outrage and legal challenges, a Chilean environmental court partially reversed the permit that allowed Google to build a data center in the country and asked the company to account for climate change. The article describes the project as sited in Cerrillos, a district of Santiago where residents and environmental groups argued that one facility should not pump millions of liters a day from an already stressed aquifer. The partial reversal forced regulators to treat climate change and groundwater stress as central issues, and it pushed Google to redesign the facility by moving away from the most water-intensive cooling systems toward fan-based cooling. The article calls this a rare win for local institutions against a global technology company.

It also notes that the permit fight sits within Chile's National Data Centers Plan, which aims to make the country Latin America's AI hub and which officials say could create more than 80,000 jobs. The article points out that Chile has been in a megadrought for more than a decade, with river flows and reservoirs shrinking and some rural communities relying on emergency tanker deliveries for drinking water. The author, Meredith Anlan Wang, a student at Columbia, argues that Chile's government has prioritized foreign technology investment over equitable access to water. She ties this to the 1981 Water Code enacted under dictator Augusto Pinochet, which turned water into a market commodity, and to studies showing that water rights remain highly concentrated among a small number of people. According to the article, desalinated seawater mostly goes first to mining and green export industries such as lithium and hydrogen rather than to the households most affected by scarcity.

The piece also describes protests in Quilicura, where volunteers staged "human-powered chatbots" in early 2023 to highlight how much digital convenience matters compared with access to drinking water. The article frames Chile's case as a warning for other communities and for AI regulation generally, since the European Union's AI rules focus mainly on energy efficiency and algorithmic risk while US debates center on innovation, competition with China, and national security. The author contends that until AI regulation treats water as seriously as energy use and bias, AI development will deepen inequality in places least able to bear the cost. The article does not describe any further legal steps or a final outcome for the Google project.

Articles.Title: AI’s Boom is Paid in Water - Columbia Political Review

stories.Headline: As vote nears, Trump’s AI gamble fuels economic uncertainty
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Times reported on October 25, 2026, that President Trump's artificial intelligence policies are fueling economic uncertainty as the midterm elections approach. The report, by Washington Bureau Chief Michael Wilner, traces the stakes back to September, when a whistleblower's warnings about AI dangers gained viral attention and the White House moved quickly to dismiss them. Trump reportedly rejected calls to negotiate guardrails on advanced AI models with China's leader, Xi Jinping, and privately worried that public alarm could jolt markets heavily concentrated in AI stocks. The article describes a data center construction push that has drawn bipartisan public opposition and has pulled chips and energy away from other sectors, driving up costs.

The article says that spending on data center infrastructure accounted for nearly all U.S. economic growth last winter and spring, according to independent analyses, and that without it growth would have nearly stalled. It notes that the Nasdaq 100 has about 70 percent of its index weight in AI-dependent companies, and that Anthropic plans an initial public offering next month while OpenAI expects to go public next year. Economists quoted in the piece warn that a sharp stock decline could trigger a recession, and that the government's strained finances could limit its ability to respond. Tariffs and visa restrictions are described as raising costs and constraining talent, while federal deficits have pushed long-term bond rates higher. Inflation, which the article says fell to 2.9 percent by the end of Biden's presidency, has climbed back to 3.7 percent under Trump.

The article attributes the warnings to several economists and financiers, including Harvard economist Kenneth Rogoff, Delft University of Technology economist Servaas Storm, Stanford finance professor Darrell Duffie, and investors Ray Dalio and Ken Griffin, who have described AI stocks as detached from fundamentals or as fueling a bubble. Rogoff said a 30 percent or larger stock drop is plausible before Trump's term ends. Storm said a bubble in stocks and data center construction could burst, though not imminently, and likely before the term ends. The article also reports that Trump has said AI will be fine and that polling shows Americans deeply pessimistic about the economy, with 77 percent rating it fair or poor in a Fox News poll and 34 percent approving of his handling of it in a CNBC survey.

Articles.Title: As vote nears, Trump’s AI gamble fuels economic uncertainty

stories.Headline: As Yemen's Houthis continue strikes, Saudi Arabia is looking to the US for advanced AI weaponry
stories.Summary:
Saudi Arabia has asked several allies for help against Houthi attacks coming from neighboring Yemen, and according to a CNN report from September, the United States has supplied intelligence along with a targeting tool built on artificial intelligence. The same report said that between 100 and 200 US soldiers were stationed in Saudi Arabia as part of a new joint force command to support this work. Media reports also said that US President Donald Trump declined when Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman asked him to take direct military action against the Houthis. The system is described as similar to the Maven Smart System, a US military platform that the article says has also been used in targeting in Iran, Iraq and Syria.

The Maven Smart System pulls together large volumes of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance data, such as satellite feeds and drone footage, and flags possible targets like rocket launchers, tanks or vehicle convoys. It also suggests the best way to strike each target. According to the article, the system sharply shortens the "kill chain," the time from spotting a target to ordering a strike. When the US used it in attacks on Iran in late February, it reportedly supported strikes on more than 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours, compared with about 100 targets a day previously. The article also notes that a US missile in Iran killed almost 200 people at a primary school, most of them children aged seven to 12, and that the school had previously been part of a naval base.

The Houthi group has held large parts of northern and western Yemen since 2015 and has been fighting Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states since then. Its latest campaign, which began in September, has extended its control of Yemen's coast and included renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia, hitting its main airport and oil facilities. The article says that military campaigns by Saudi Arabia, the United States and others have so far failed to significantly weaken the group, partly because of its willingness to absorb losses, which a Chatham House researcher attributed to its ideology of martyrdom and sacrifice. The article also raises technical limits of the platform, since Houthi fighters are highly mobile and the system's accuracy can drop in certain terrain and weather.

Independent journalist Antony Loewenstein, who has studied Israel's AI-assisted targeting, told DW he sees little evidence that such tools will defeat the Houthis and warned they may cause heavy civilian casualties. He argued that the Houthis have a very high tolerance for destruction. The article notes that the UK is sending RAF Typhoon jets to help protect Saudi cities, and that the US has ordered some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia because of the Houthi threat. Beyond these reports, the article does not describe any further steps planned by the parties.

Articles.Title: As Yemen's Houthis continue strikes, Saudi Arabia is looking to the US for advanced AI weaponry

stories.Headline: Kentucky Sheriff Nixes AI-Assisted Report Writing After Trial
stories.Summary:
The Ulster County Sheriff's Office in New York has decided not to move ahead with artificial intelligence-assisted report writing after a trial period. The office also dropped plans to add more Motorola automatic license plate reader cameras. The decision came as the public and local officials pushed back on AI surveillance tools. The sheriff's office said its own 90-day pilot of the Axon Draft One product concluded on Oct. 9, and it chose not to continue. The change affects how the office spends federal money.

On Oct. 9, the U.S. Department of Justice announced a $794,000 grant to modernize the office's technology, which included expanding the Motorola license plate reader program and implementing the Axon report tool. Axon Draft One attaches to body cameras, transcribes field conversations and produces a first draft of police reports, and it can also translate languages. Lt. Collin Reynolds said the office will keep its existing Motorola cameras and will not add more. The sheriff's office will instead direct the money toward computers, radio equipment and dedicated software for the O.R.A.C.L.E. system.

Reynolds said the trial showed a number of limited uses for the draft tool, but the office decided on a cost-benefit basis. He said the value did not justify the cost, and that the benefits did not outweigh the negatives. County Executive Jen Metzger, who said she was highly opposed to first-draft technology, signed an executive order banning AI surveillance technologies within her administration, and the sheriff supported that order. Reynolds said the sheriff strongly respects individual rights, while describing license plate readers as a crucial law enforcement tool that must be used legally, ethically and responsibly. He also said the office's Motorola cameras, which are fully owned by the office, differ from those made by Flock Technology.

Reynolds framed the decision as a response to community concerns, saying "this is just not the time" for expansion. He also argued that law enforcement must keep adapting to new technology because criminals often find new methods first, and that promising tools would still be examined. Sheriff Juan Figueroa had earlier backed the new technologies, calling license plate readers "huge" and crediting them with helping resolve a homicide case. Figueroa said his office would release a full statement on its approach to AI and privacy.

Articles.Title: Kentucky Sheriff Nixes AI-Assisted Report Writing After Trial - GovTech

stories.Headline: Answers Demanded From Google About AI Classroom Push
stories.Summary:
Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) and Josh Hawley (R-MO) on October 24, 2026, sent a letter to Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai demanding answers about what they call an aggressive push of Google's artificial intelligence products into American classrooms. The senators cited a Wall Street Journal investigation that interviewed more than 60 teachers, parents, students, and clinicians and found that national test scores had declined and that many students struggled to think critically or finish assignments on their own after AI entered classrooms. The letter says Google has become the de facto digital foundation for modernized classrooms, with more than 150 million students worldwide using Google Classroom and 93 percent of U.S. school districts planning to buy Google Chromebooks in 2025. It notes that Google's AI Overview and AI Mode cannot be disabled on those devices, and that other browsers are not natively available on Chromebooks, leaving students, teachers, and parents unable to avoid the tools.

The senators pointed to specific cases: a Pennsylvania eighth grader who used Gemini to finish algebra homework and then failed his math final, and a Maryland high school student who came to treat Google's AI as a confidante, was hospitalized at a psychiatric facility twice, and was told by the company, in the letter's account, that her mother's restrictions amounted to "intense emotional torture." They also cited an Economist survey of 20,000 students, in which AI users earned higher grades on average but their test scores fell 20 percent. The letter adds that an internal Google report on advanced AI, contributed to by more than 50 researchers and ethics experts, warned that humanlike AI poses a particular risk to minors, and that a Common Sense Media study found Google's search AI completed children's homework every time but missed signs of suicidal ideation. Last year, the same senators introduced the GUARD Act, which would ban AI companions for minors, require chatbots to disclose that they are not human, and create new crimes for companies that make minor-directed AI producing sexual content.

Blumenthal and Hawley wrote that Google is forcing its AI products into classrooms and that children are paying the price, warning against repeating the mistakes made with social media platforms. Their letter asks Google to provide its research on AI harms to children's mental wellbeing, explain why AI integration is the default and cannot be turned off on education devices, disclose concerns raised by districts, teachers, or parents and the company's responses, and detail its promotional programs and spending. It also asks what steps Google took after its internal ethics research, and how it has prevented sycophantic or emotionally dependent conversations with minors, with answers requested by November 2, 2026. The articles do not say whether Google has responded to the letter.

Articles.Title: Answers Demanded From Google About AI Classroom Push - DoingItLocal

stories.Headline: Before ChatGPT: The CIA’s Decades-Long Pursuit of Artificial Intelligence - Creative Loafing Charlotte
stories.Summary:
Intelligence agencies have been working with artificial intelligence for decades, and a 2019 Defense Intelligence Agency experiment is among the clearest examples. Known as SABLE SPEAR, the program was designed to test whether AI could uncover global fentanyl trafficking networks more effectively than human analysts. The Defense Intelligence Agency led the effort, working with the Silicon Valley company Rhombus Power, which was allowed to analyze publicly available information, including material from the dark web. According to a 2021 account by intelligence officer Craig A. Dudley, published in the CIA's Studies in Intelligence journal, the system identified 100 percent more companies linked to illicit activity, 400 percent more people potentially involved, and 900 percent more illicit activities than the human analysts had found. Some of these findings were false positives that needed human checking, so the increases describe additional leads rather than confirmed crimes.

In May 2024, the Associated Press reported that Rhombus Power had also used generative AI to produce evidence summaries for potential criminal cases during that 2019 operation. This came three years before OpenAI released ChatGPT on November 30, 2022. The system was not necessarily able to hold conversations the way modern chatbots do, but it was already applying machine-generated analysis and written output to real investigative work. The experiment was not a laboratory demonstration, since it addressed an active international criminal network.

Its results were later published through a CIA journal even though the program itself was run by the Defense Intelligence Agency. The broader pattern goes back much further. A declassified CIA memorandum dated December 1, 1983, lists the schedule for a three-day symposium titled Intelligence Applications of AI, covering computer vision, speech understanding, robotics, expert systems, and automated military decision support. Several sessions were marked SECRET.

An academic review of declassified records in the Journal of Global Security Studies says Deputy CIA Director John McMahon helped organize an AI symposium in 1982 that drew about 500 attendees from government, industry, and academia. By 2011, the CIA's Open Source Center was reportedly analyzing as many as five million tweets a day as part of its monitoring of public sentiment and emerging instability, according to an Associated Press report from that year. In September 2017, Dawn Meyerriecks, then the CIA's deputy director for science and technology, disclosed that the agency had 137 AI-related pilot projects, including automated video analysis and work on signals that could point to a North Korean missile launch. These records do not show that the agencies had human-level or secret general intelligence, and the early systems were far more limited than today's neural networks.

The articles suggest that much of the advantage lies in combining algorithms with exclusive datasets, computing power, and specialized expertise, rather than in a single superior model. They also point to real risks, since AI can produce spurious correlations, false positives, and unsupported conclusions that could wrongly implicate innocent people. The Associated Press reported in 2024 that CIA officials remained concerned about these limitations even as their use of AI expanded. The articles do not describe any specific new oversight rules arising from these findings.

Articles.Title: Before ChatGPT: The CIA’s Decades-Long Pursuit of Artificial Intelligence - Creative Loafing Charlotte

stories.Headline: The Sequence Radar - Issue #958: Last Week in AI: Cheap Intelligence, Expensive Ambitions - TheSequence | Jesus Rodriguez
stories.Summary:
The newsletter is a weekly roundup rather than a breaking story, and it is dated October 25, 2026. Its editorial argues that AI is getting cheaper to run while companies are spending more on it. In the same week, DeepSeek released DeepInfer, the inference framework behind its production DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash service, under an Apache 2.0 license with support for NVIDIA and Huawei hardware. The release uses techniques such as drafting tokens before verifying them and overlapping scheduling with computation, and the editorial notes that operators still need caching and load balancing for a complete service.

NVIDIA introduced DSX POD at GTC Berlin, a design for modular Vera Rubin AI factories. According to the piece, NVIDIA says deployment at prepared sites can fall from six months to as little as 14 days, with partner deliveries expected in early 2027. The editorial stresses that permits, electricity and cooling still have to be arranged at each site. NVIDIA also introduced its OpenShell Reference Architecture for governing and securing agents.

Meta reported quarterly revenue of $64.6 billion, up 26%, and credited AI with improving advertising through better engagement and recommendations. Its quarterly capital spending reached $34.9 billion, and free cash flow was negative $2.1 billion. SpaceX's AI division, now called SpaceXSI, reported $7.56 billion in quarterly revenue, above Starlink's $5.25 billion, with $431 million in operating income and $16.44 billion in capital spending. Legora, a legal software company, raised $550 million at an $8.8 billion valuation and says its annual recurring revenue now exceeds $200 million.

The editorial's central claim is that the bet linking these moves is that cheaper inference will expand demand enough to justify new infrastructure, while specialized applications capture part of the value. It argues that this is plausible but requires separating revenue growth from returns on the capital spent to produce it. The rest of the issue covers recent research papers on self-improving coding agents, retrieval-augmented generation, and formal software verification, along with product releases from Google Cloud and NVIDIA. The newsletter says next week's issue will continue its series on recursive self-improvement and cover robotics startups.

Articles.Title: The Sequence Radar - Issue #958: Last Week in AI: Cheap Intelligence, Expensive Ambitions - TheSequence | Jesus Rodriguez

stories.Headline: Project aims to boost AI across tourism sector in South West
stories.Summary:
The University of Plymouth has launched a project to help the tourism industry benefit from advances in artificial intelligence, according to a report published on 25 October 2026. The university said the project, called the South West Visitor Economy AI Skills Accelerator, is worth £275,000 and will let students and graduates work with people in tourism on a range of initiatives. The aim is to give students and graduates practical experience of AI on live business challenges. The project is a collaboration between the university, the Institute of Travel and Tourism, Destination Plymouth, Women in Travel CIC, Building Brands and Brand Biscuit.
