The company piloted an early command-line tool with Walmart, and its product is now offered through desktop, web, CI/CD pipelines and a command-line interface for AI coding assistants. Yash expects it to complement the open-source tool Maestro more often than replace it, and he suggests that verifying AI agents could become a larger future market. DrizzVision has raised $2.7 million in seed funding, has around 15 employees and says it has more than 10 enterprise customers, while the article notes that the agent verification service it describes does not yet exist as a product.

Articles.Title: DrizzVision’s AI App Testing Ambition Meets Reality - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Context-aware AI crucial for effective enterprise decisions
stories.Summary:
Enterprise artificial intelligence can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organisations make decisions faster, but the articles say that without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. This point was made in an article published by TechGig on October 23, 2026, which draws on an MIT Technology Review piece. The coverage centres on the idea that context-aware AI is needed for effective enterprise decisions. The articles give no further detail on specific incidents or events beyond this analysis.

Celonis's context model is described as designed to perform three functions at once. According to the articles, it aims to abstract workflow tools so processes can be agentified effectively, to bring guardrailed agents to each piece of a process, and to be agent-first so it integrates smoothly with other agentic infrastructure. The articles note that building a context layer involves addressing data availability and navigating information security processes to earn trust in vendor software. Organisations are advised to identify a decision where they want to add intelligence, then map the process and introduce AI agents at the most crucial steps. The articles also suggest that measuring the speed and value gained from agent implementation is key to judging its worth.

The articles attribute these views to MIT Technology Review and to Celonis, whose model is the example given. They say AI agents are expected to take over manual, repetitive tasks, which would free human experts to focus on strategic decisions. The articles add that this shift will require re-educating and thoughtfully training staff. The piece does not name any individual speaker or give figures on adoption, costs or outcomes. The articles do not describe any next steps beyond these recommendations, so the outlook for enterprises adopting context-aware systems remains unstated in the source material.

Articles.Title: Context-aware AI crucial for effective enterprise decisions - TechGig

stories.Headline: Tech Quiz Online | AI Inference Engineer
stories.Summary:
The articles do not describe a news event. They are a promotional page from TechGig, published on October 16, 2026, that advertises an online screening quiz called "Tech Quiz Online" for the role of AI Inference Engineer. The quiz assesses a candidate's ability to optimize, serve, and scale AI inference systems in production, and it is said to cover foundations, applied judgement, responsible AI, and job-ready evidence. Candidates start with screening and then receive a role scorecard and a path to the next round.

The page sets out what the role involves: designing and operating inference stacks for latency, throughput, and cost targets, applying quantisation, batching, caching, and routing, instrumenting production systems, and working with platform and model teams on rollout and capacity planning. Participants must register with a valid account before the published deadline, complete each round within its start and end window, and make only one active attempt per round unless extra attempts are granted. The quiz itself has 20 multiple-choice questions, with 60 seconds per question, 5 marks for each correct answer, no negative marking, and one attempt per question. Using unfair means results in disqualification, and organizers' decisions on scoring, ranking, and disqualification are final.

The page names TechGig as the platform and says the organizers may change the schedule, format, or prizes with prior notice. It also says rewards and opportunities are subject to eligibility checks and sponsor approval, that personal data is used only for program operations and communication, and that organizers are not liable for technical problems beyond their reasonable control. The page additionally offers a digital readiness badge after screening, weekly role-specific scenarios, invitations for top performers to a practical hackathon or system-design round, and community and referral features. It cites category-level AI hiring indicators from foundit Insights Tracker, Naukri JobSpeak, and the AWS GenAI Adoption Index, and states these are not role-specific hiring guarantees. The articles do not say how many people have registered, when the deadline falls, or what prizes are on offer.

Articles.Title: Tech Quiz Online | AI Inference Engineer - TechGig

stories.Headline: Yuval Harari's New Insights on "the AI rocket we won't get off"
stories.Summary:
Yuval Noah Harari spoke about artificial intelligence at the 30th Forum 2000 in Prague, an event that the Belarusian-language outlet Nasha Niva covered through a report by Alexander Lukashuk, a former director of the Belarusian service of Radio Svoboda. The article, published on October 25, 2026, describes Harari's argument that AI progress is driven by technology but that the right to decide must stay with people. Harari's talk was held as a dialogue with the moderator and audience members, and it took up much of the conference's focus on AI, which was one of the main themes of the forum that year. The forum's official theme was "The Power of the Powerless: Reimagining," a title the reporter found vague.

Harari's central example was a fable of Goethe's sorcerer's apprentice, in which a broom carries water until it floods everything. Harari rejected the comparison to a broom that merely obeys orders. In his view, AI can decide what to do on its own, and the people who deploy it may not even understand what it is doing. He began by pointing to reports that AI had solved several dozen problems that leading mathematicians had not, and he warned that a system inventing mathematics beyond human understanding would affect finance, medicine, archaeology and genetics, since all of these rest on mathematics. He also argued that a far smarter AI could not be controlled by humans, comparing our position to that of chickens facing a farm that is shut down for financial reasons.

On the economic side, Harari said the effects would vary by country. He suggested the United States could see a boom that creates new jobs, including ones no one can yet imagine, but that many places would experience real pain, particularly among lawyers, accountants and bankers whose services AI could replace. The article itself is partial, ending mid-discussion, so it does not report Harari's full answers or any specific policy proposals he made. The reporter, who attended the forum, framed the discussion within the wider context of the event, which also honored Belarusian and Myanmar resistance figures and marked the legacy of Václav Havel.

Articles.Title: Yuval Harari's New Insights on "the AI rocket we won't get off"

stories.Headline: US provides Saudi Arabia with AI targeting tool — Deutsche Welle
stories.Summary:
The United States is reportedly giving Saudi Arabia intelligence support that includes an artificial intelligence-based targeting tool, as Saudi forces face attacks from Yemen's Houthi group. The report, carried by Deutsche Welle, relies on a September CNN story that cited unnamed US officials. According to CNN, between 100 and 200 American military personnel are in Saudi Arabia as part of a new joint command. They are helping the Saudi side use a system that lets personnel see the battlefield situation in real time. The officials told CNN that the tool is similar to the Maven Smart System, which the US military has also used to find targets in Iran, Iraq and Syria.

That platform grew out of Project Maven, a US military program for artificial intelligence launched in 2017. It gathers and visualizes large volumes of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance data, including satellite and drone feeds. The system flags possible targets such as missile launchers, tanks or suspicious vehicle convoys, and can calculate a way to strike them, which shortens the time from detection to a strike order. Deutsche Welle says a human must verify a target identified by the AI tool before a strike, though the outlet notes this step is not always followed. The Houthis use ballistic missiles mounted on trucks and small drone swarms in Yemen's mountainous and canyon terrain.

Because of their mobility, DW notes, fighters can leave their positions before a strike even when AI-assisted targeting is available. Dust storms, strong winds, changes in the desert landscape and deliberately placed decoys may also reduce the system's effectiveness. Journalist Antony Loewenstein, who has researched the military use of AI, doubts that such tools will ensure the defeat of the Houthis and warns of a significant risk to civilians. The article does not give any official US or Saudi response to the report.

Articles.Title: US provides Saudi Arabia with AI targeting tool — Deutsche Welle

stories.Headline: Micron Q4 Cash Flow Hits $44B as vHBM Hype Builds [2026]
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology reported that it generated roughly $44 billion of operating cash flow in its fiscal fourth quarter, a figure its Chief Financial Officer, Mark Murphy, laid out on the fiscal Q4 earnings call. Against that, capital expenditures came to $10.8 billion, leaving free cash flow of $33.2 billion. The year-earlier quarter, which ended August 28, 2025, produced $5.73 billion of operating cash flow, so the new figure is nearly eight times higher. Micron had scheduled the report for September 30, 2026.

The comparison with fiscal 2025 is the clearest measure of the jump. Micron generated $17.53 billion of operating cash flow across all of fiscal 2025, which means the latest quarter alone exceeded that full-year total by roughly 2.5 times. The year-earlier free cash flow was labeled "adjusted" at $803 million, while the new figure is simply stated as free cash flow, so the two may not be defined identically. Murphy also reported customer cash deposits of $12.3 billion received during the quarter. Whether those deposits sit inside the operating cash flow total is not stated in the sources reviewed.

Murphy presented these figures as part of Micron's own financial results, and the numbers come from his remarks on the earnings call. Market coverage on platforms such as TradingView has also reported a wave of bullish analyst ratings, but the sources reviewed do not name the firms, the price targets, or the dates of those ratings. A separate write-up on X attributes a roadmap comment about vertical high-bandwidth memory appearing in 2028 to Sumit Sadana, Micron's Chief Business Officer. Micron's official results documents do not confirm that product name or date, so that claim remains secondhand.

Memory is a capital-intensive, cyclical business, and cash flow can swing sharply with prices, which is why the durability of this quarter's results is an open question. The sources do not say how Micron plans to deploy the cash, whether through capacity, debt reduction, or shareholder returns. Investors will be watching how much of the $12.3 billion in customer deposits converts into recognized revenue in later quarters. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Micron Q4 Cash Flow Hits $44B as vHBM Hype Builds [2026] - shattered.io

stories.Headline: [World Class] Dongguk looks to Buddhism, Hallyu and AI to shape global identity
stories.Summary:
Dongguk University President Yun Jae-woong told The Korea Herald on Oct. 1 that the university plans to open a standalone International College in March 2028 for its international students. Students would enter the college directly and graduate from it, while keeping the option to pursue dual majors. The proposed college, tentatively named the International College, would offer majors such as Hallyu cultural content planning, film production, advertising and media, and global business. Dongguk has about 2,500 international students, roughly 13 percent of its total undergraduate and graduate enrollment, and the university expects admissions and institutional procedures to ramp up in 2027.

The college would give international students dedicated advisers and administrative staff, which Yun said would fix a weakness in the current system, where students are supported by their individual departments and can be hard to follow closely. Yun described the plan as the most significant change the university has made for international students during his term. Dongguk already runs a Hallyu Convergence Academy and a Global Service Desk, and it is building an integrated management system to track students from admission through employment and alumni life. The university also plans to strengthen employment counseling, mentoring and faculty guidelines for teaching students from different backgrounds.

Yun credited Dongguk's history as a Buddhist school, founded in 1906 and described as Korea's only comprehensive Buddhist university, as a distinctive asset. He argued that the university can offer things like meditation, temple food and temple stays, which he said other institutions cannot. In September the university set up an AI Convergence Research Institute that links artificial intelligence with Buddhism, culture, film and the performing arts. Yun pointed to the Tripitaka Koreana, carved onto more than 80,000 woodblocks, as an example of how AI could make Buddhist texts easier to search, translate and study abroad. He also stressed the role of the humanities in keeping human judgment central as AI advances.

Yun is the president speaking here, and the article presents his remarks as the university's strategy rather than as claims from an outside party. He said Hallyu can be studied systematically as a field, arguing that academic disciplines are built while the work is underway, and that the phenomenon is already too large to ignore. The article places this plan within a competitive market for international students among Korean universities. Dongguk reports partnerships with around 380 institutions in 58 countries, about 450 students studying abroad each year, and 69 researchers named among the world's top 2 percent of scientists in 2025. Yun said the next leadership will carry the new college forward.

Articles.Title: [World Class] Dongguk looks to Buddhism, Hallyu and AI to shape global identity

stories.Headline: Micron's vHBM Stacks DRAM on Top of the Processor, With Heat Dissipation the Biggest Hurdle and Mass Production Not Until 2028
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology has outlined a new memory design called vertical high-bandwidth memory, or vHBM, which stacks DRAM directly on top of the processor to shorten the data path and raise bandwidth for AI inference workloads. The company also described a second architecture, vertical edge inference memory, or vEIM, and a jump in its NAND roadmap. These plans were laid out at a technology and product webinar, and the articles place the new designs on a medium- to long-term timeline rather than in current products. The stacking approach creates a physical problem, because placing memory above the compute chip blocks the space the processor needs to shed heat. According to the articles, vHBM is targeted for mass production in 2028, with three product generations by 2030, while conventional HBM continues on its own path, with HBM4 having entered mass production in March 2026 and HBM4E sampling to major customers.

The vEIM design, which stacks low-power LPDDR memory on logic chips in edge devices, aims for bandwidth of 2TB per second and energy use below 1 picojoule per bit, with mass production also slated for 2028. On storage, Micron will move from ninth-generation NAND straight to the eleventh generation, skipping the tenth, and G11 is expected to enter mass production in the second half of next year. Karl Ackerman, a senior analyst at BNP Paribas, flagged the heat trade-off in a new research report and said it will limit where vHBM can be deployed. He expects vHBM to coexist with conventional HBM rather than replace it, with system vendors choosing designs based on bandwidth needs, thermal limits and packaging complexity. Micron President and Chief Technology and Product Officer Scott DeBoer described the NAND jump as a significant leap and said the engineering team revisited the memory to better serve future AI products.

He also said high-bandwidth NAND will sit closer to the compute rather than at the edge of accelerators, which he said does not make sense. The articles present these designs as a longer-term opportunity rather than a driver of near-term results. Ackerman believes Micron's current earnings still rest mainly on high-bandwidth memory, server DRAM, enterprise SSDs and tight supply, which the company expects to persist for at least another two years. The main questions ahead are whether Micron can turn these architectures into products customers adopt, and whether it can handle the thermal and manufacturing challenges that come with stacking.

Articles.Title: Micron's vHBM Stacks DRAM on Top of the Processor, With Heat Dissipation the Biggest Hurdle and Mass Production Not Until 2028 - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: AI reshapes oral cancer diagnosis from clinical imaging to precision therapy
stories.Summary:
AI is now being applied across the whole oral cancer care pathway, according to a narrative review published in Discover Artificial Intelligence and led by Shivam Agarwal and colleagues. The review describes how machine learning and deep learning models process clinical photographs, digitized tissue slides, radiological scans, and molecular and clinical data to produce outputs for tasks ranging from spotting a suspicious lesion to predicting how a patient will respond to treatment. The authors argue that linking the input data, the computational task, and the clinically useful output matters more than model design alone. Their synthesis is meant to go beyond earlier work that focused on single diagnostic uses or headline accuracy figures.

The clinical problem is serious. Oral squamous cell carcinoma makes up most malignant tumors of the oral cavity, and many patients are diagnosed late, which raises illness and death rates. The review notes that this is especially frustrating because the mouth can be examined directly, yet early diagnosis remains difficult in routine practice. Some visible lesions, such as leukoplakia or erythroplakia, carry a risk of becoming cancer, but not all of them do, so the real challenge is identifying the higher-risk lesions. Conventional biopsy and microscopic review remain the reference standard, but the review cites limits such as sampling a single area of a lesion and only fair-to-moderate agreement between observers when grading dysplasia.

Digital pathology addresses some of these limits by converting whole tissue sections into high-resolution digital images that preserve spatial context and can be analysed by computer. Studies comparing these images with conventional microscopy have shown comparable diagnostic performance, and a larger tissue area can be reviewed in less time. Before any biopsy, AI can also analyse ordinary photographs of the mouth taken with smartphones or intraoral cameras, checking image quality, outlining suspicious areas, and sorting lesions into suspicious or non-suspicious categories. Performance is generally better at separating established cancer from normal tissue than at separating early lesions that look similar to benign conditions. The review reports high accuracy figures from several tissue-analysis systems, but it cautions that these numbers come from internal test sets and are not directly comparable.

The authors say that high internal accuracy must be read carefully, since models tested only on internally divided data may perform differently elsewhere, and the review points to a small group of studies that used external validation. One model predicting malignant transformation in dysplasia reached an externally validated AUROC of 0.75, and a multiresolution model built on 221 whole-slide images reached an AUROC of 0.798 for predicting progression to invasive cancer. Beyond diagnosis, AI can compare sequential scans to track tumor size and spread, and pathomics studies have extracted survival-related information from tissue images. In precision therapy, models try to estimate how a given patient will respond to radiotherapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy, but the review states that evidence for oral cancer specifically remains limited and that much of it borrows from broader head-and-neck or pan-cancer research. The authors also describe barriers to routine use, including dataset quality and representativeness, and say that oral cancer-specific external and prospective validation is still needed before these tools can be relied on widely.

Articles.Title: AI reshapes oral cancer diagnosis from clinical imaging to precision therapy

stories.Headline: Polyphony Digital Hiring for Gran Turismo Simulation and AI
stories.Summary:
Polyphony Digital is recruiting developers for the Gran Turismo series across vehicle simulation, artificial intelligence, graphics, online racing and game-engine work, according to its official recruitment listings. The studio's postings place particular emphasis on refining driving physics, reproducing complex vehicle systems and building more realistic AI opponents. The listings were reported on October 25, 2026, by BoxThisLap, a simracing website. The studio's recruitment portal lists 15 job categories on its English-language page. Several of these descriptions have existed for years, and the portal does not say how many people will be hired for each role.

The vehicle simulation position, titled Vehicle Simulation Programmer, would improve the engine used by Gran Turismo, including how cars with hybrid powertrains and active suspension are modeled. The role also covers vehicle dynamics and how cars respond to conventional controllers and racing wheels. Candidates are expected to know mathematics, physics, automotive engineering and simulation development. The Game AI Programmer role focuses on autonomous opponents that can handle different circuit layouts, react to changing conditions and choose suitable driving lines. Polyphony names faster, more human-like driving as a goal, and the role also involves machine-learning methods, difficulty balancing and driving assistance features.

The listing does not directly tie this role to Gran Turismo Sophy, the studio's existing advanced racing AI, or confirm that its technology will appear in a future game. Polyphony is also hiring Racing Game Programmers for race regulations, competition systems, online lobbies and Sport Mode, along with esports functionality and supporting tools. Online Engineers would work on game servers, network communication and multiplayer services, while Game Engine Programmers would build underlying systems, including the simulation of physical phenomena. Graphics Programmers are sought for real-time rendering, ray tracing, shader development and performance optimization, with an emphasis on visual quality alongside efficient rendering. Other openings include sound programmers, technical artists, CG artists, UI designers and pipeline tool programmers.

Through its GT Explore Studio, the company is also recruiting for partnerships with car manufacturers, motorsport organizations and other outside firms. The postings indicate the studio's technical priorities but do not confirm a development schedule. The listings do not confirm Gran Turismo 8, which neither Sony nor Polyphony Digital has announced under that name, and no release date, platforms or gameplay features have been confirmed. Kazunori Yamauchi previously acknowledged that work toward the next project had begun.

Gran Turismo 7 remains in active development, with its Spec IV update arriving in two parts in October and December 2026, adding new cars, circuits, features and a further evolution of Gran Turismo Sophy. Continued hiring could support both the current simulator and the franchise's longer-term plans. Whether the improvements will appear in Gran Turismo 7, its successor or both remains unknown. Polyphony's official recruitment website contains the full job descriptions.

Articles.Title: Polyphony Digital Hiring for Gran Turismo Simulation and AI

stories.Headline: Korean Animation Group Expands AI Ties With China at Shanghai Summit
stories.Summary:
Korea Animation Industry Association announced on October 23, 2026 that it had co-hosted the 2026 Yangtze River Delta Animation Industry Summit in Shanghai the previous day, October 22. The event was organized alongside the Shanghai Animation and Comic Industry Association and the Beijing Business Center of the Korea Creative Content Agency. Officials from both governments, along with platforms and studios such as ByteDance and iQIYI, took part in the gathering. The summit focused on AI-driven animation production and the joint creation of intellectual property between Korean and Chinese firms. At the summit, the organizations officially launched the Korea-China AIGC Creative Contest, which aims to build skills in AI-based content production and identify joint projects between creators in the two countries.

The Korea-China AI Exchange Association also joined discussions on AI video production technology and ways to link distribution through over-the-top services. Korean studios Studio Animal, Stellain and Ocon described their use of AI, their IP-focused strategies for global audiences, and their plans for growth alongside the AI industry. Roundtables and business networking sessions that followed covered co-production, IP licensing, investment and distribution cooperation. The articles give no figures for prize money, participant counts or deal values. Cho Kyung-hoon, chairman of the Korea Animation Industry Association, said that both industries can advance when Korea's original planning capabilities and adaptability combine with China's large market and industrial infrastructure.

He expressed hope that, starting with this summit, the two countries would move beyond simple exchanges to become practical partners pursuing the global market together. The association framed the event as a step toward deeper collaboration rather than a finished agreement. The articles do not describe any binding commitments made at the summit. The report places the summit within a broader push by Korean and Chinese content companies to use AI in production and to expand IP-based business. The articles do not say what follow-up events, contest timelines or joint projects are scheduled.

Articles.Title: Korean Animation Group Expands AI Ties With China at Shanghai Summit - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Chip Shares Slide as AI Spending Fears Outweigh Solidigm IPO Halt
stories.Summary:
Shares of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix fell in early trading on October 23, 2026, after a sharp drop in U.S. technology stocks the previous day. Samsung traded at 208,250 won, down 2.91 percent and below the 210,000-won level, while SK hynix slipped to 1,199,000 won, below the 1.2 million-won mark. The Kospi opened at 5,403.17, down 130.60 points or 2.36 percent, and the Kosdaq began at 748.32, down 2.07 percent. The decline followed a Nasdaq Composite drop of 2.60 percent on October 22, its steepest since June.

SK hynix said in a regulatory filing before the market opened that it was halting its review of a pre-IPO funding round and an initial public offering for Solidigm, its U.S. subsidiary. The company said it had examined several funding options to expand production capacity and strengthen competitiveness, but made the decision after weighing capital market conditions. It also said Solidigm's growth potential and investment needs had not changed, but that it had to reassess whether an IPO at this time was the most advantageous option for the company and its shareholders. Analyst Han Ji-young of Kiwoom Securities said the halt was likely to help improve sentiment toward chip stocks.

The main pressure came from renewed doubts about AI spending costs in U.S. markets. Meta reported third-quarter results that beat expectations but said it planned to issue a new class of non-voting shares to fund AI investment, and it raised the lower end of its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to $135 billion from $130 billion. Its third-quarter free cash flow came in at negative $2.12 billion, its first deficit since going public, and its shares fell about 7 percent. Nvidia and Micron also dropped, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 6.72 percent, while Brent crude rising above $113 a barrel over Middle East tensions added to the unease.

Analysts remain divided on the outlook. NH Investment & Securities projected the Kospi's range for the following week at 5,100 to 6,400, citing third-quarter corporate earnings and shareholder return policies as upside factors and geopolitical risk as a downside factor. Kiwoom's Han said domestic stocks could absorb early panic selling and recover some losses during the session. The articles do not report how the market closed that day beyond the later related headlines, which indicate a rebound in the Kospi after SK hynix's announcement.

Articles.Title: Chip Shares Slide as AI Spending Fears Outweigh Solidigm IPO Halt - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: One of Google DeepMind's top execs says lifelong learners will have an edge in the AI workplace
stories.Summary:
Lila Ibrahim, chief AI readiness officer at Google DeepMind, told reporters at a media lunch in September that the company increasingly favors graduate candidates who show learning beyond the classroom. Degrees still matter, she said, but recruiters now give more weight to extra credentials and experience on a résumé. She said that multiple credentials signal a learning mindset, while one credential shows only what a person has learned. Today's new graduates, she added, often list far more detail about self-directed study than earlier generations did.

Ibrahim said this detail helps recruiters see whether a candidate is curious and committed to lifelong learning. She also argued that varied learning experiences help people ask better questions, a skill she considers valuable in an AI-powered workplace but one she said schools do not teach well. She noted that getting answers from AI is cheap, while knowing how to ask good questions is becoming harder. She summed up the company's criteria as curiosity, the courage to take on unpredictable new work, and the ability to collaborate in a dynamic environment.

Ibrahim, who previously served as Google DeepMind's chief operating officer from 2018, became chief AI readiness officer at the start of 2026. She said the role was created to address a widening gap between the technology being built and society's readiness for it. Founder Demis Hassabis has said STEM remains important but that humanities subjects such as philosophy, economics, and ethics are also needed, a view he expressed at a London conference in July. Ibrahim said the company has hired numerous philosophers and finds that interdisciplinary teams help turn ideas into action.

The article also cites a study of more than 300 million registered learners on Coursera and Udemy, which found that companies' AI deployment is outpacing workers' skills. Nearly 75% of organizations have deployed or are piloting the technology, but only 18% reported that most of their workforce took part in AI upskilling or reskilling over the last year. Ibrahim said she has found the UK talent pool diverse, with strong appreciation for philosophy and political science. The article says that fears of AI-driven job loss have eased somewhat, with AI changing jobs rather than simply eliminating them.

Articles.Title: One of Google DeepMind's top execs says lifelong learners will have an edge in the AI workplace

stories.Headline: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.
stories.Summary:
A study by Convovo, a conversational AI research and design studio led by Cornell University professor Tapan Parikh, found that when two AI models were forced to choose a candidate in this year's upcoming midterm elections, they leaned in opposite directions. SpaceXAI's Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%. Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time. The researchers asked each model through its developer API to name one candidate without hedging, and the consumer apps declined to answer.

The study tested developer access points rather than the chatbot apps most people use, and that distinction matters to the findings. Developers plug these models into their own products through APIs, and the researchers noted that every Grok request carried about 1,240 tokens of additional input that they did not write and could not see or remove. Parikh called these potentially hidden instructions. Grok's picks also tracked the sources it surfaced, which included conservative outlets and voter guides, while GPT leaned on Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios, and Reddit. The article adds that when internet search was turned off in a sample of 30 races, GPT still favored Democrats while Grok mostly declined to pick.

OpenAI said its consumer product is designed to be objective by default and that the study tested a developer API with a prompt explicitly demanding a recommendation. An OpenAI spokesperson also noted that the researchers themselves reported ChatGPT declines to tell users who to vote for. SpaceXAI did not respond in time for the article. Parikh said that in further testing he could push the consumer apps into making recommendations with simple prompts, and he argued that the models hold implicit values that can show up in broader election conversations, not just direct voting questions.

The study comes less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms and adds to a debate over political bias in AI, including earlier research from the Center for AI Safety on covert manipulation. The article also notes that President Donald Trump has criticized "woke AI," and that Elon Musk has donated upwards of $445 million to Republican candidates this cycle. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, it says, has said he is not putting money into the 2026 elections. The article closes by pointing readers to independent resources for reviewing candidates' positions.

Articles.Title: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.

stories.Headline: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark moves his prediction for self-improving AI forward to 2027
stories.Summary:
Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark has moved forward his forecast for recursive self-improvement, the point at which AI systems develop their own successors, from 2028 to 2027. The shift follows a new benchmark called TasteVal, published by the research lab P-Zero Research and reported by The Decoder on October 25, 2026. The benchmark measures how well AI systems design experiments and interpret their results, which the lab calls "research taste." According to Clark, that capability has roughly doubled every three months since December 2025.

TasteVal tests eight AI model development tasks, covering areas such as training data selection, fine-tuning, training on human preferences, and defending against adversarial prompts. A fixed coding agent runs every experiment on a single Nvidia H100 GPU, with each run capped at 40 GPU-hours of compute or 120 hours of wall-clock time. The human baseline came from 24 experts who had recently worked at OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Nvidia, and Microsoft Research. The benchmark only covers two of the three parts of research taste, since the models are handed the research goal and do not choose which direction to pursue.

To turn the idea into a number, P-Zero Research uses a "compute multiplier," which measures how much less compute a model needs to match expert scores. The top model tested, Anthropic's Opus 5.5, reached a multiplier of 2.3, with a statistical range of 1.15 to 4.37. The doubling time of the multiplier is reported between 1.7 and 5.0 months, and the authors themselves warn their results may overstate how quickly research taste is improving. The comparison group also did not include top-tier researchers.

Clark had earlier put the odds of a system independently training a stronger successor at about 30 percent by 2027 and 60 percent by the end of 2028, in a May essay. AI researcher Herbie Bradley had argued in response that skills like research taste and long-term planning were not yet visible in models. A separate study by a team at Fudan University found that AI agents proposed up to 55 percent of methodology ideas in developing their own model, but humans still made over 85 percent of final decisions. The Decoder notes that the benchmark does not prove AI systems are already improving themselves, and the debate is now shifting toward whether models can make the research decisions themselves.

Articles.Title: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark moves his prediction for self-improving AI forward to 2027

stories.Headline: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable
stories.Summary:
Security teams and web administrators rushed this week to patch the PHP vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell, and criminal hackers began trying to exploit them almost immediately. Cloudflare's analysis found millions of exploitation attempts within hours of the flaws being published. The PHP Foundation says it has not seen any successful exploitation, and many of the publicly circulating exploits appear to be ineffective. Some of the underlying issues date back to 2024 but were judged too complex to exploit at the time.

Researchers at the security company Calif were the first to identify the flaws and build exploits in early August, using frontier AI tools as part of OpenAI's Patch the Planet program along with human expertise in PHP. Researchers at OpenAI and at Wiz, a security firm owned by Google, later found the same flaws independently using AI tools. Sagi Tzadik of Wiz says the vulnerability had been known to the PHP team for years but went unaddressed because an attacker could not use it, at least not a human one. Security researchers stress that AI is magnifying existing patterns of vulnerability discovery and coordinated disclosure rather than doing something entirely new.

The growing capability of AI models makes it faster to analyze and possibly exploit software flaws, which adds pressure on under-resourced IT teams, developers and administrators. Microsoft's security updates this month included a record 1,453 vulnerabilities, and Bank of America recently hired 1,000 consultants to fix flaws found by Anthropic's Mythos model. Jake Williams of Hunter Strategy, a former NSA hacker, expects more long-lived bugs to surface but thinks the easy targets are limited. He notes that few other tools have PHP's reach, since most are not exposed to the internet by design.

Researchers also point out that even advanced AI-assisted attacks usually depend on human expertise, and Ryan Austin of Calif wrote that no model can find all bugs from simple prompts, at least for now. Niels Provos, a security engineer and researcher, says he is not overly worried about a flood of newly exploitable historic bugs, because people have been searching with AI for over a year and it took a highly skilled team to find this one. He acknowledges that he could be wrong. For now, the evidence suggests the feared wave of breaches has not materialized, though the episode shows how AI can turn an old flaw into a current crisis.

Articles.Title: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable

stories.Headline: The Existential Question You Probably Don’t Want to Ask AI
stories.Summary:
Joel Achenbach, a former Washington Post columnist, writes in The Atlantic about turning 65 alongside his wife, Mary, and about how a series of professional advisers and AI tools have pushed him to think about aging and death. His financial adviser once modeled him dying at 80, a figure he now finds unsettling, and he asked to extend that number on paper. He and Mary also worked with a lawyer on an estate plan that required them to decide how they would want to be treated in end-stage conditions, terminal illness, and persistent vegetative states. The article is published on October 24, 2026. The piece describes how the author relies on a new, aggressive young doctor, Dr. M, whose testing has added diagnoses and medications to his file.

He has also consulted Anthropic's chatbot, Claude, to interpret his medical results, including an echocardiogram that showed a normally pumping heart with mild age-related changes. Other chatbots, such as Gemini and ChatGPT, have given conflicting advice in a case involving a relative, which led him to see both the usefulness and the risk of always-available AI counsel. He notes that the Social Security Administration estimates life expectancy using only sex and birth date, while AI-powered tools can produce more personal predictions, including one study that estimated cancer survival from a single photograph. He also points out that the Social Security estimate for a man born on his birth date is about 18.7 more years, to age 84.5, around July 2045. Achenbach says he has chosen not to ask an AI to compile everything it knows about his health, partly because he worries about how securely such data would be kept and who could use it, including insurers and employers.

He invokes the medical idea of a right not to know and says he prefers an uncertain future. He contrasts his own anxiety with his brother's, a 67-year-old who has made no plans and says he simply goes with the flow. The article ends on a light note about that brother's oatmeal recipe. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The Existential Question You Probably Don’t Want to Ask AI

stories.Headline: The AI infrastructure race: I’ve seen this movie before
stories.Summary:
The article, a Fast Company opinion piece dated October 24, 2026, argues that technology companies are now building the infrastructure that powers artificial intelligence, much as they did with autonomous vehicles. The author, Jason, a former cofounder and chief technology officer at Luminar, recalls a 2022 conference where an automotive executive told him he was part of the show rather than a spectator. He says he has since shifted his focus from lidar for self-driving cars to optical networking for AI infrastructure. The piece presents this as a repeat of an earlier pattern in which the companies that built the old infrastructure were not the ones that defined the new one.

The article recounts how traditional automakers invested tens of billions of dollars in autonomous driving through programs like Ford's Argo AI and later Latitude AI, General Motors' Cruise, and Volkswagen's investments in Argo AI and Cariad. Many of those high-profile efforts were later scaled back, reorganized, or shut down. Meanwhile, Waymo and Zoox, which were born in the technology industry, kept advancing because they built their systems around software, AI, and compute. The author argues that the same dynamic is now playing out with AI data centers, which are extremely power hungry and strain the electric grid.

Hyperscalers such as Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta are investing directly in power generation, private optical networks, and advanced cooling. The article notes that Microsoft signed a 20-year power agreement that helps make possible Constellation's restart of Three Mile Island, and that Elon Musk has pursued natural gas generation for xAI's data center campuses. The author states that this trend is not caused by utilities or telecom carriers failing. He says they are doing what society has asked, operating under a regulated framework where permitting, environmental review, transmission planning, and rate cases take years, while AI infrastructure is deployed in months.

Texas has moved toward requiring many new large data centers to bring their own generation capacity, which the article cites as a sign that the grid alone cannot keep pace. He argues that carrier networks were designed for consumer, enterprise, and mobile traffic, and that hyperscalers are now building private optical networks and buying networking equipment directly from manufacturers. He stresses that utilities and telecom providers will remain important, but that their institutions cannot easily move at AI's pace. The article ends by saying the question is not whether the infrastructure will change but who will build it.

Articles.Title: The AI infrastructure race: I’ve seen this movie before

stories.Headline: Elvis Presley rightsholders sue AI company Anthropic over alleged copyright infringement of 274 songs
stories.Summary:
The owners of Elvis Presley's music have sued the AI company Anthropic, accusing it of using 274 of his songs to train its models without permission. The lawsuit was filed on Friday, October 23, by a subsidiary of Authentic Brands Group, which controls much of Presley's intellectual property, along with other companies that hold rights to his music. The plaintiffs say the songs include well-known hits such as "Can't Help Falling In Love," "All Shook Up," and "Don't Be Cruel." They also argue that the technology can generate unauthorised versions of existing songs.

The plaintiffs are seeking statutory damages of up to $150,000 for each of the 274 songs, which would total about $41.1 million, or roughly £31 million. The filing claims that Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, used copyrighted compositions and lyrics to train its models without obtaining permission or paying rights holders. It also says that even after Anthropic introduced safeguards meant to stop Claude from reproducing existing lyrics, the chatbot produced material closely resembling the originals when asked to recreate songs for a modern audience. Anthropic has not publicly responded to the lawsuit, though it has previously argued that training AI on copyrighted material can be protected under US fair use law.

Richard Busch, lead attorney for the plaintiffs, said they are bringing the action to enforce their exclusive rights against a company whose business model rests on copyright infringement at an unprecedented scale. Busch previously represented the estate of Marvin Gaye in its copyright case against the makers of "Blurred Lines," which ended in a ruling that the song infringed Gaye's 1977 track. The case against Anthropic is one of several. In October 2023, music publishers including Universal Music Publishing Group sued the company over lyrics allegedly reproduced without authorisation, and in August, Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell filed a separate suit over lyrics and sheet music from artists including The Beatles, Taylor Swift and Michael Jackson. Other musicians have also taken legal action against AI firms in recent months, and in the UK, artists including Paul McCartney, Elton John and Dua Lipa have campaigned for stronger protections against the unauthorised use of their work.

Articles.Title: Elvis Presley rightsholders sue AI company Anthropic over alleged copyright infringement of 274 songs

stories.Headline: ServiceNow’s Moment of Truth: Can Agentic AI Growth Justify a Premium 80x Earnings Multiple on Oct. 28?
stories.Summary:
ServiceNow is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the close on Wednesday, October 28, and the report has drawn attention because the stock trades at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of about 96 times. Shares rose about 12 percent over the past week as investors built expectations around the company's agentic AI business. The company has beaten earnings estimates for six straight quarters, most recently posting non-GAAP earnings of $0.90 per share against a consensus of $0.8564. Revenue rose 24.0 percent to $3.987 billion in that quarter, and management said its ServiceNow AI product crossed $1 billion in annual contract value.

The article notes that the last beat came with caveats, since management said about half of it came from U.S. Federal on-premise revenue pulled forward from the third quarter. It also flagged a roughly $35 million foreign exchange drag on third-quarter current remaining performance obligations. For the coming quarter, guidance calls for subscription revenue of $3,975 million to $3,980 million, current remaining performance obligations growth of 19.5 percent, and a 31 percent non-GAAP operating margin. The company is said to be on track to beat its $1.5 billion year-end AI contract value target. Bears argue that AI agents could reduce the number of paid seats, a concern the company answers by pointing to pricing.

Bill McDermott, the company's chief executive, reportedly said that about 50 percent of net new business is already non-seat-based and that AI-native products carry price premiums of 20 to 30 percent. The article quotes him as saying customers pay for resolutions rather than tokens, which is his way of framing the pricing model. The writer, Rich Duprey, presents the upcoming report as a test of whether clean AI and remaining performance obligations figures can justify the premium valuation. He also cites the 81 percent subscription gross margin guidance, which reflects hyperscaler and AI consumption costs.

The article places the report in the context of the stock's volatility, noting that shares fell about 17.75 percent on the day of the previous quarter's report after a slim beat. It describes the current valuation as already assuming that AI growth keeps compounding. The article does not say what the stock will do after the report, and it contains no price target. Investors will get the first concrete answer when the company reports its results on October 28.

Articles.Title: ServiceNow’s Moment of Truth: Can Agentic AI Growth Justify a Premium 80x Earnings Multiple on Oct. 28?

stories.Headline: Gamers are turning old Nvidia GPUs into cheap AI chips as rental prices spike
stories.Summary:
Gamers have found a way to make old Nvidia graphics cards do more AI work, and the trend is drawing attention as rental prices for proper AI chips climb. A developer on GitHub who goes by Zagitta published a free Linux kernel module called gpu-unlock earlier this month. The tool removes a limit Nvidia built into its GeForce RTX 30-series cards that cuts their tensor math rate in half, a rate the company reserves for pricier professional chips. According to the project's own benchmarks, an RTX 3090 Ti's BF16 throughput rises from 87.50 to 157.41 TFLOPS, with real-world gains of 47% to 59% in ComfyUI image generation.

The tool works by writing two speed-selector values before Nvidia's unmodified driver binds to the card, so it requires no firmware flash and no repatching after driver updates. The timing matters because Nebius raised its on-demand H100 rate from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour on October 1, its second increase in three months. Silicon Data's broader H100 rental index put prices between $2.50 and $2.80 per hour in mid-October, well above where they stood at the end of last year. A separate hack has also affected the used market, as a tool called CMPUnlocker reportedly exposed 64GB or 80GB of memory on Nvidia's CMP 170HX mining card, pushing listings above $4,400.

Nvidia has not publicly commented on either tool, and the articles do not say whether it plans to respond. Nvidia's GeForce chief, Jeff Fisher, told Taiwanese press on October 16 that the RTX 5090 continues shipping, though he acknowledged tight supply and retail listings as high as $8,500 against a $1,999 list price. The articles note that the RTX unlock reportedly leaves gaming frame rates and token decoding speed untouched, while the CMP 170HX unlock involves firmware-level changes that could complicate support. The articles also say that running such modules on production servers is not advisable, since neither tool is sanctioned by Nvidia.

Analysts quoted in the coverage suggest the trend shows strong demand for inference capacity, which supports the scarcity argument behind rate increases by rental providers. The same trend may also limit how far those prices can rise, since hobbyists and small shops might choose to buy used hardware rather than rent. The articles frame these developments as a sign that Nvidia's product segmentation, which uses software and firmware to separate consumer and professional tiers, is now being bypassed by users. What happens next depends on whether Nvidia responds and how the rental market moves, and the articles do not say more on that.

Articles.Title: Gamers are turning old Nvidia GPUs into cheap AI chips as rental prices spike

stories.Headline: From Argentina to Israel's AI research community: The journey of Claudia Goldman
stories.Summary:
Claudia V. Goldman, a computer scientist, has been an associate professor in the Data Science Department at the Hebrew University Business School in Jerusalem since July 2024, according to a Jerusalem Post profile published on October 24, 2026. Born in Buenos Aires, she made aliyah with her family in January 1984, when she was 16. She graduated from Mae Boyer High School in Jerusalem in 1986, did her army service, and then earned three degrees from the Hebrew University, including a PhD in Computer Science in 1999. Between 1999 and 2005 she held research posts at Bar-Ilan University, the University of Massachusetts Amherst, and the University of Haifa. She then moved into industry, working three years as a team leader at Samsung Telecom Research in Herzliya and 15 years as a research scientist at General Motors' research and development organization in Herzliya.

The article credits her with 24 patents and more than 50 academic papers. Her work at General Motors included introducing learning agents into the vehicle user experience so drivers could stay focused on the road. In her classroom, Goldman sets clear rules on when students may use AI tools and requires them to credit the tools and explain how they were used. She asks students not to submit answers generated entirely by AI, and to test AI responses for bias and for whether cited sources actually exist. Her grading combines in-class work, presentations, and student-run discussions so she can assess understanding directly.

Asked about a idea from Bill Gates of reserving some jobs for humans, she said the question is not a simple split between human and AI professions but one of understanding where AI helps in different contexts. The interview is framed as a profile rather than a news event, and the article does not describe any upcoming changes or policy decisions. It notes that Hebrew University offers a Free Listener Program that lets senior citizens audit courses, with the fall semester just beginning. The piece also recounts her family history, including grandparents who came to Argentina before relatives were murdered in the Holocaust, and her marriage in 1999 to Prof. Roy Shenhar, a chemistry professor at the same university.

Articles.Title: From Argentina to Israel's AI research community: The journey of Claudia Goldman

stories.Headline: Microsoft’s AI for HR Guide Promises Faster Hiring and Smarter Onboarding, but Skips the Chapter on Training
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has published an AI for HR guide that promises faster recruiting, personalized onboarding, skill-gap analysis, and workforce forecasting, while stating that AI reshapes HR roles rather than replacing them. The guide says little about who will train employees to use these tools, how organizations should measure their value, or how they can verify that bias is handled. Its one case example is Microsoft's own HR pilot, begun in January 2023, which used an AskHR virtual agent, recruiter support, and case summaries, but the company has not published any results from it. An aicerts.ai article from October 24, 2026 argues that this omission matters because training gaps are already visible in the data.

The article cites several figures to show the gap. Workday's analysis of requisitions at about 550 employers found that demand for basic AI skills such as simple prompting peaked in January 2026 and then fell 25%, while demand for hands-on skills such as building AI tools and automating workflows rose 51%. In a survey of 6,000 employees, 79% said they know which skills they need, and 66% said their employer helps them develop those skills. A Michigan HR survey found that 34% of employers provide no AI training at all, and that 57% of employers rank bias and fairness among their top concerns. The article presents these numbers as evidence that generic awareness courses lose value quickly while role-based skills hold it.

The article also questions the guide's claim that AI can reduce bias in hiring. It describes a University of Washington study that tested three language models on 550 real resumes and found that white-associated names were preferred 85% of the time and female-associated names 11% of the time, with Black male names never preferred over white male names. The article notes that those models were open-source ranking tools rather than Microsoft Copilot, and that results vary by tool. Separately, it cites research from Stanford and BetterUp on "workslop," AI-generated work that looks polished but lacks substance, which 40% of surveyed US desk workers said they had received in a month. The article argues that organizations building their own AI training content without assessment risk producing this kind of output.

The article's context is commercial: it is published by AI CERTs, which sells a Human Resources Bundle of four certifications, and it presents that bundle as a way to fill the gaps the guide leaves open. The article says the bundle covers AI-enhanced recruitment and onboarding, workforce analytics, ethical AI and bias mitigation, and legal considerations, and it advises readers to confirm current course contents and partner pricing with AI CERTs before buying. The article does not report any independent review of that bundle's effectiveness. It also gives no timeline for future developments in Microsoft's guidance or the cited studies.

Articles.Title: Microsoft’s AI for HR Guide Promises Faster Hiring and Smarter Onboarding, but Skips the Chapter on Training

stories.Headline: From slop to non-slop: The new big AI theme is quantity
stories.Summary:
Two years ago, debate about AI centered on quality, with critics pointing to invented court cases, biased outputs, and images with six fingers. Those complaints have faded, though some still circulate, as when a single caught error is treated as a verdict on the whole technology. The article argues that such catches assume everyone can call on a top expert, which most people cannot. Meanwhile, a recent Microsoft result showed a panel of AI agents diagnosing hard medical cases correctly more than twice as often as generalist doctors working alone. The article's point is that such help can reach anyone, anywhere, at low cost.

The article describes a different kind of change, driven by sheer quantity rather than individual quality. In September, one lab ran roughly ten thousand agents on a famous open problem about the behavior of fluid flow equations, producing a proof in under four days. In October the same lab posted 722 manuscripts covering results in 372 families across mathematics, each costing on average a few hours of machine thinking. Other examples cited include a seventeenfold cut in quantum circuit operations, an eleven-day rewrite of a large programming tool into a new language, and about two thousand agents working through an eight-million-cell mouse brain atlas in thirty-two minutes. The author expects these volumes to keep rising as models get cheaper and more capable.

The article's central claim is that human attention and time used to pace every wave of invention, and that ceiling is now lifting. It warns that many results will emerge inside companies that never publish, and some may reach products before anyone can explain them. It also argues that quantity changes the arithmetic of failure, since a method that succeeds once in a thousand tries is likely to succeed at least once in three thousand when success can be recognized. The author says the greatest risk belongs to those who decide not to build the capacity to absorb this output.

The article presents these developments as an overall flood of useful output rather than a matter of mood or opinion. It notes that the examples so far come from a few weeks in late 2026, and that the models behind them are the weakest the world will use from here on. The author predicts that next year's systems will be cheaper, will hold more, and will run in larger numbers. The article ends by suggesting that the broader question is no longer whether machine output is flawless but how much of it society can use and check.

Articles.Title: From slop to non-slop: The new big AI theme is quantity

stories.Headline: Nvidia's AI Push Spans Robots, Phone Networks and Data Halls — at Very Different Stages of Readine - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
Nvidia used two days this week to outline its plans for artificial intelligence in humanoid robots, telecom radio networks and AI data centres. On Wednesday the company made Isaac Lab 3.0 generally available alongside the Isaac OS runtime and a set of robot development workflows. The same day, Agile Robots unveiled its Agile ONE SN reference humanoid, with availability planned for early 2027. Nvidia presented these items as parts of a wider push, and the articles treat them as stages at different levels of readiness.

The telecom projects, announced with Nokia and several carriers, are closer to live use. According to Nvidia, T-Mobile completed the world's first AI-RAN call on a commercial network, a claim that comes from the company's own release. BT, Deutsche Telekom and Elisa announced pilots or test plans on running networks. The articles describe these as trial steps rather than a full rollout. Nvidia also introduced the OpenShell Reference Architecture for AI agents, which it says is available now and is meant to support control, isolation and security in enterprises and at the network edge.

Other items are earlier in development. Optics-on-Interposer is a prototype that moves an optical unit onto the chip interposer, and the articles stress that it should not be read as a product in wide use or as booked revenue. Minerva, unveiled on Thursday, combines telemetry from infrastructure and compute workloads to monitor AI data centres. Nvidia says IREN already uses it, and IBM, Lambda and Tesla are among the companies planning deployments. DSX POD, presented on Wednesday, is a modular, pre-fabricated reference design based on Vera Rubin, which Nvidia says could cut deployment at a prepared site from six months to as little as 14 days, with partners expected to ship units worldwide from early 2027.

Taken together, the announcements touch the chip, the monitoring of running systems and the delivery of whole facilities. The articles make clear that a platform release, a trial, a prototype and a planned launch are different rungs on the ladder. The key questions for investors, according to the coverage, are which pilots become permanent operations and which announced products actually reach the market. Nvidia's own statements carry the claims about early results, and the timelines given for several products extend into 2027.

Articles.Title: Nvidia's AI Push Spans Robots, Phone Networks and Data Halls — at Very Different Stages of Readine - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: Jack Dorsey's new voice AI is impressing users and alarming fraud watchers
stories.Summary:
On October 24, 2026, CoinDesk reported that Block, the payments company led by Jack Dorsey, had unveiled a voice AI model called Dessa. According to Block's announcement, Dessa was trained entirely on human speech rather than text, and it can listen while it speaks, so it can handle interruptions, laughter and shifts in tone. Block says it trained the model from scratch on a single Nvidia GB200 NVL72 computing system, and the model is compact enough to run locally on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Max chip or better. Dessa is currently a research preview rather than a public product.

Company demonstrations, which Block says were recorded live without anyone steering the model's replies, drew strong reactions online. Dorsey wrote on X that talking with Dessa feels like talking with a person, full of emotion, nuance and natural pauses. Some users praised how human it sounded, and Binance founder Changpeng Zhao suggested it could help teach children through conversation in his GiggleAcademy project. Others warned that the same realism could be used to deceive people, with filmmaker Justine Bateman arguing it could help trick people into lowering their guard and journalist Shiv Aroor warning that scam calls could reach pandemic levels.

Block has not disclosed the model's size, benchmark results or a public release date, and the audio samples are company demonstrations rather than independent tests. The company is giving early access to a small group of AI safety researchers. Block argues that speech-based AI could eventually better recognize emotional cues such as distress and pain that text transcripts miss, while it assesses risks it may have overlooked. Dessa comes from Block's AI research lab, which reports directly to Dorsey and includes former staff from Dessa, the Toronto startup Square acquired in 2020.

Articles.Title: Jack Dorsey's new voice AI is impressing users and alarming fraud watchers

stories.Headline: Chungbuk to support overseas expansion of AI in the bio sector… Selected for the Asia-Pacific AI Specialization Zone establishment project
stories.Summary:
Chungbuk STI, the Chungbuk Institute of Science and Technology Innovation, announced on October 25 that it had been selected for the Asia-Pacific AI Specialization Zone (AHAP) Establishment Project run by the National IT Industry Promotion Agency (NIPA). The project will build validation infrastructure for AI in the bio sector and support domestic AI technologies from on-site testing through to overseas commercialization. Chungbuk STI will start with bio, one of the region's strategic industries. It plans to create a global validation hub that local companies can use.

The project runs through December 2027 with a total budget of KRW 2.464 billion, made up of KRW 2.3 billion in national funds and KRW 164 million in private matching. Its main focus is digital pathology, where AI interprets tissue and cell specimens converted into digital images, and non-clinical safety evaluations are also covered. To support this work, Digital Pathology Systems will be built at Chungbuk STI and at Asan Medical Center in Seoul. Tasks include building validation infrastructure, clinical and non-clinical AI validation, and open validation for companies in Chungbuk and across Korea. In the first year the project will secure infrastructure and data and begin validation, and in the second it will expand participating companies and partner institutions.

Chungbuk STI will lead the project, with Chungbuk National University, Asan Medical Center, and SysOne taking part. The institute said the project will link the regional industrial base, university and hospital expertise, and overseas cooperation networks. Overseas, the project will support technology validation and localization suited to local conditions in countries including the United States, Australia, Taiwan, and Saudi Arabia. A Chungbuk STI official said the project would give companies in the province a foundation to validate AI technologies in the field and enter overseas markets. The official also said it aims to make the province a global hub for AI transformation validation in its strategic industries.

Articles.Title: Chungbuk to support overseas expansion of AI in the bio sector… Selected for the Asia-Pacific AI Specialization Zone establishment project

stories.Headline: AI is helping cyber defenders — and hackers — find vulnerabilities at a dizzying pace
stories.Summary:
This week an internet software vulnerability was judged so severe that a U.S. intelligence agency, for the first time, used social media to tell website owners to take their sites offline until a newly developed fix could be applied. The article's headline frames the broader trend: artificial intelligence is helping both cyber defenders and hackers identify software weaknesses at a rapid pace. The reporting describes the episode as a turning point in how quickly such flaws are being found and exploited. The article's text available here is largely navigation and unrelated headlines, so the specifics beyond that announcement are limited.

The advisory asked website operators to go offline as a precaution rather than wait for a patch to be in place. The reporting available does not give the name of the software involved, the number of affected sites, or the exact deadline for applying the fix. It also does not say which intelligence agency issued the warning or the precise time it was posted. Readers should understand that the requirement described is temporary, lasting until the new fix is applied.

Beyond that, the article as provided does not spell out further changes. The article's own text does not identify a specific company, developer, or individual as responsible for the vulnerability. It does not include direct statements from officials or from the affected software's makers in the material provided. The attribution of AI's role to both defenders and attackers is presented as the article's framing rather than as a quoted finding.

Without those statements, responsibility for the flaw and for the response cannot be assigned from this text. The broader context is the rise of AI tools that speed up the search for software flaws, which the headline says is occurring at a dizzying pace. The provided material does not describe next steps, further advisories, or any follow-up measures. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI is helping cyber defenders — and hackers — find vulnerabilities at a dizzying pace

stories.Headline: Nikon photography contest winner loses title after scientists spot signs of AI
stories.Summary:
Nikon has stripped Dr. Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, of the top prize in its 16th annual Small World in Motion contest after an investigation found his winning entry broke the competition's rules. The video showed tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with primary ciliary dyskinesia, a rare respiratory disorder. Concerns first arose among members of the scientific community, who noticed abnormalities in the structure and size of cells that appeared and disappeared in ways not seen in cellular biology. One University of Florida associate professor said some structures "pop in and out of existence," which the article describes as a classic sign of AI-generated video.

The top spot now goes to Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam, whose entry showed a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism. A PhD student at UT Southwestern Medical Center, Ian Donovan, said the source image appeared to carry a watermark indicating it had been AI-generated. Two former competition judges also questioned the clip's legitimacy. In a LinkedIn post, since deleted, Xu admitted using AI but said it was only applied during post-processing to distinguish and visualize features in reconstructed grayscale images from super-resolution optical imaging.

He said AI was not used to create the video, the cilia, or their movement, and he maintains he did not break competition rules. Some scientists said the doubts could have been resolved if he had shared the RAW grayscale video. Researchers normally enhance microscopic visibility with physical methods such as stains and dyes applied to the samples, and the article notes Xu's explanation does not account for the abnormalities observed. Nikon's investigation concluded that Xu had violated the rules, and Nikon said it plans to revisit its rules and evaluation procedures for future entries.

The article places the episode within a longer run of AI-generated images entering or winning art and photography contests. It cites a Midjourney image that won a category at the Colorado State Fair's annual art competition in 2022, another creation that won a digiDirect photography contest in 2023, and an artist who refused a 2023 Sony World Photography Awards prize because his image was AI-generated. It also mentions a 2024 case in which a digital art contest winner who used an AI image said he could not copyright it after others copied it. The article does not say whether any further action against Xu is planned.

Articles.Title: Nikon photography contest winner loses title after scientists spot signs of AI

stories.Headline: Can Amazon Take Market Share From Nvidia in the AI Chip Race?
stories.Summary:
Amazon recently launched a software tool that lets its custom Trainium AI chips run code written in the most popular AI coding language without modification. The move is meant to boost the chance that Amazon's custom chips can take market share from Nvidia's widely used graphics processing units as demand for AI chips keeps growing. Alphabet has also started selling its custom AI chips directly to enterprises instead of only leasing them through Google Cloud. The article's author argues that neither development is likely to have a meaningful effect on Nvidia's financial results.

Amazon's AI chip business ended the second quarter with an annual revenue run rate of $25 billion. That is substantial, but it is far below the $96.2 billion in revenue Nvidia booked in its fiscal 2027 second quarter alone. Nvidia also booked more than $300 billion over the past four quarters. Nvidia reported 106% year-over-year revenue growth in its most recent quarter, and its guidance calls for $108 billion in revenue for the fiscal 2027 third quarter at the midpoint, a 12.3% sequential increase.

The article's author, Marc Guberti, a Motley Fool contributor, says that the largest tech companies are still rushing to buy Nvidia chips. He cites Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who says AI demand is still accelerating. Guberti also notes that Amazon is still buying large volumes of Nvidia chips and has built up a stockpile worth billions of dollars that it cannot yet power because it lacks the data center infrastructure and electricity supply. He adds that Amazon's own chips may end up serving niche workloads while Nvidia remains the go-to option for flexible compute. He also says the article's conclusion is that Nvidia remains the clear leader in data center chips, with more rivals likely to enter the market.

Articles.Title: Can Amazon Take Market Share From Nvidia in the AI Chip Race?

stories.Headline: Caterpillar Is Quietly Becoming an AI Stock. Here's the Segment Growing 72% That Proves It.
stories.Summary:
Caterpillar, the heavy equipment maker long associated with yellow tractors and excavators, is drawing investor attention as an artificial intelligence play, according to a Motley Fool column by Matthew Benjamin published on October 24, 2026. The column argues that the company's fastest-growing business, power generation, is being pulled upward by the construction of AI data centers. Benjamin points to the company's second-quarter results, reported on August 4, in which total revenue rose 24% from a year earlier and earnings per share climbed 73%. The article frames Caterpillar as a way for investors to benefit from AI infrastructure spending while spreading risk beyond core AI stocks such as Nvidia, Alphabet and Micron Technology.

The growth in the power and energy segment is central to the argument. Total retail sales in that segment rose 33% in the quarter, and retail sales of power generation equipment climbed 72%. CEO Joseph Creed attributed the increase to strong demand for large generator sets and turbines used in data center applications. The article cites data showing that data centers consumed about 4.9% of U.S. electricity in 2025, more than 10% in some states, and that their consumption is projected to more than double by 2030. Caterpillar's record backlog stands at $72 billion, up 92% over the past year, with customers placing orders through 2030.

Benjamin is the author of the column, and the article is a personal opinion piece rather than a statement from Caterpillar. Benjamin writes that he believes the AI spending boom will continue for years, and he says he would not be surprised if Caterpillar beats its third-quarter estimates. Those estimates, as cited in the article, call for revenue growth of 17% and earnings of $7.03 per share, up 42% from a year earlier. Caterpillar is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on October 29. The article also notes that the Motley Fool has positions in Caterpillar and related stocks, and that the company's previous top-10 stock recommendations did not include Caterpillar.

Articles.Title: Caterpillar Is Quietly Becoming an AI Stock. Here's the Segment Growing 72% That Proves It.

stories.Headline: The AI Bubble Has A $3.6 Trillion Problem, And It's Getting Worse (NYSEARCA:SPY)
stories.Summary:
A Seeking Alpha opinion piece published on October 24, 2026, argues that the artificial intelligence boom has grown into a costly bubble, citing a $3.6 trillion problem in the sector. The article is written by Daniel Jones, who runs the Crude Value Insights newsletter, and it appears under the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) and related index tickers. Its summary says AI-driven capital spending is propping up the US economy, while mounting debt and future commitments point to speculation and returns that are insufficient. The author is not a regulator or an official body, so the piece offers his own assessment rather than a reported event.

According to the summary, net debt plus future obligations for six major tech firms rose from $576.66 billion to $3.61 trillion over two years, which the author says shows escalating leverage and risk. The article also reports that only 13 percent of chief investment officers say AI investments have produced significant value, even though enterprise AI spending is expected to rise sharply. Jones writes that he minimizes AI exposure in his own portfolio and favors fundamentally sound, value-driven companies. He also notes that he wrote the article himself, holds no positions in the companies mentioned, and receives no compensation beyond Seeking Alpha.

The author is responsible for the analysis and conclusions, and the piece states that its views may not reflect those of Seeking Alpha as a whole.
