stories.Headline: how to verify if your site blocks ai crawlers
stories.Summary:
Many websites block AI crawlers without meaning to, and the cause is often a security plugin, a content delivery network setting, or an outdated robots.txt file. According to a TechGig article published on October 14, 2026, this can stop AI assistants from quoting a site's pages, which reduces the site's visibility in AI-generated answers. The article, which appeared on the site's technology section, is aimed at website administrators who want to find out whether this is happening to them. The first check is the robots.txt file, which sits at the root of the domain. Administrators should look for entries that disallow specific AI user agents, since a crawler follows the most specific group that names it, so a dedicated GPTBot group overrides general wildcard rules.

A line reading Disallow: with nothing after it blocks nothing, while Disallow: / blocks everything for that agent. Because firewalls, bot-protection plugins, and CDN settings can refuse a request before robots.txt is ever read, the article also recommends sending a request that identifies itself as a crawler, using a tool such as curl. A 200 status code suggests access, while 403, 406, or 429 indicates a block from a component in front of the site. Server or CDN logs give the definitive picture because they record the actual codes crawlers received. The article distinguishes two kinds of AI crawler that administrators need to treat differently.

Answer fetchers, such as OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot, retrieve pages to answer user questions, while training crawlers, such as GPTBot and ClaudeBot, collect content for model training. A site may choose to allow answer fetchers to preserve visibility while blocking training crawlers, and robots.txt can express that choice by allowing the first group and disallowing the second. Any firewall or CDN rules must then be adjusted to match. The article also cautions that allowing access only means a crawler can read the content, and it does not guarantee that an AI assistant will recommend the site, since recommendations depend on the content's relevance.

Articles.Title: how to verify if your site blocks ai crawlers

stories.Headline: build ai agents with function calling using python
stories.Summary:
A new tutorial published by TechGig on October 14, 2026, walks readers through building a complete AI agent framework from scratch using Python. Its central technique is function calling, sometimes called tool use, which lets large language models output structured JSON that invokes predefined functions. The guide frames this as the step that turns an LLM from a text generator into something that can take actions. The tutorial is aimed at developers who want to build such systems themselves.

The framework is organized around several concrete tools. These include a WebSearchTool for querying the web, a PythonExecutorTool for running code, and a CalculatorTool for math operations. It also provides FileReadTool and FileWriteTool for handling files, and an agent core that manages communication with the model, runs the tools, and keeps conversation context across multiple turns. The code supports both the OpenRouter and Groq APIs and uses free-tier models, including google/gemini-2.0-flash-exp:free and llama-3.1-70b-versatile. The article does not give a price or a license for these services beyond describing them as free tier.

The tutorial stresses several practices for reliable agents. Developers are advised to write clear tool descriptions, validate parameters strictly with JSON Schema, and handle errors so that tools return strings rather than raising exceptions. The framework also caps the number of turns to guard against infinite loops. A PersistentAgent class is introduced to give agents memory that carries across interactions. The article does not describe any other recommended practices beyond these.

The piece is a technical how-to rather than a news event, so it names no company or official as responsible for a decision and reports no statements from individuals. It does not describe any changes to regulation, pricing, or product policy. The article gives no indication of follow-up plans or future versions of the framework. Readers who want the full code and examples are directed to the original tutorial.

stories.Headline: langgraph guide building stateful multi step ai agents
stories.Summary:
A practical guide published by TechGig on October 14, 2026, lays out how to build stateful, multi-step AI agents using LangGraph, an extension of LangChain. The approach uses graph-based orchestration so that agents can keep memory across multi-turn conversations, run complex workflows with decision points, and recover from errors. The guide says LangGraph offers built-in state persistence, full control over branching, native debugging, and parallel execution, which set it apart from traditional LangChain Expression Language chains. It is aimed at developers who want structured control over how an agent moves from one step to the next.

The guide describes three core concepts that structure an agent. State is a shared data structure that flows through the graph, Nodes are functions that process state and return updates, and Edges define the control flow between nodes, either conditionally or unconditionally. A full example builds a ReAct agent with tools for web search, calculation, and weather information. It also covers short-term memory within a conversation thread using MemorySaver, and long-term memory across sessions using SqliteSaver. For sensitive actions, it explains human-in-the-loop approval flows that rely on interrupt and Command.

The guide further explains how to build multi-agent workflows in which specialized agents, such as researchers, writers, and editors, are orchestrated by a router function. It also discusses streaming of tokens and state for real-time updates, along with debugging and visualization tools such as draw_graph. For production use, it provides a checklist covering error handling, rate limiting, observability through LangSmith tracing, validation with Pydantic, execution timeouts, and strict state schema validation. Advanced patterns include parallel tool execution with ThreadPoolExecutor, dynamic tool selection based on query type, and reflection or self-correction mechanisms. The article notes that these agents can be deployed with a FastAPI server or in Docker containers.

stories.Headline: theygent builds local first agent platform with two plane architecture
stories.Summary:
TheYgent has introduced a local-first agent platform that places the inference engine directly inside the product, according to a company blog post reported by TechGig on October 14, 2026. The stated aim is to remove the need for an intermediary vendor between users and their AI models. The system is split into two components, an inference plane and a control plane. The inference plane handles engine processes, model weights and API credentials, and runs wherever the user configures it.

The control plane orchestrates agents, covering graph runtime, agent registries, sessions and triggers, and it never imports an engine directly. Instead it reaches inference only through the inference plane's OpenAI-compatible HTTP API, so prompts and images go straight to the inference plane. When an agent runs, the control plane sends model calls by logical ID, such as triage-fast, rather than by engine name. The inference plane starts engines on demand at the first call to a logical ID and keeps a resident ceiling, evicting the least recently used engine when it is full. Idle engines shut down after fifteen minutes, though models can be marked for continuous warmth.

The company's own documentation, as described in the article, lets users rebind a logical ID to a different engine or hosted API through a single registration update, without changing the agent. The platform offers two runtimes, an interactive in-process interpreter for live streaming and a durable runtime built on DBOS for unattended tasks. The durable runtime journals workflow state into Postgres so that a crashed run can resume from its last completed step, giving exactly-once execution for finished steps and at-least-once for steps in flight. Every run also produces spans and per-node inputs and outputs stored in the user's Postgres for observability, with an optional OpenTelemetry export that is not required. The company says it publishes a full list of its network connections and operates fully offline once installed, with no usage analytics.

stories.Headline: audit ai generated apps with seven security checks before production
stories.Summary:
AI-generated applications should go through a seven-step security audit before they reach production, according to security guidance reported by TechGig on October 14, 2026. The push follows a Veracode 2026 GenAI Code Security Report finding that AI models pass an average of only 56 per cent of security tests. The generated code usually compiles and runs, yet working code is not necessarily safe, since AI coding tools are less reliable on record visibility, malformed requests, and key exposure. The audit covers secrets, access control, database rules, dependencies, injection and input handling, LLM features, and rate and cost limits. The checks are concrete.

Developers should scan repository history for leaked passwords and API keys with tools such as gitleaks, and confirm that secret keys never reach the browser. Access control testing means creating two users, replaying one user's request with the other user or no session, and treating any returned record as an insecure direct object reference. Database rules need row-level security enabled on every exposed Supabase table, and Firestore should not run with open test rules in production. Dependencies should be checked with npm audit and npm audit signatures, and each package an assistant adds should be reviewed by hand.

Queries should be parameterised rather than built from strings, LLM features should be tested against the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, and per-user rate limits, monthly spend caps, and usage alerts should be added. The reported research behind these steps points to two patterns: exposed data from default settings and hallucinated package names. An UpGuard study published in late September 2026 examined 300,000 domains using Supabase and found 16,326 databases with publicly readable tables, which UpGuard linked to row-level security being off by default for tables created through the API. Supabase responded that projects are secure by default and that customers control their configurations.

A USENIX Security 2025 paper tested 16 models on 576,000 code samples and found hallucinated package names in 5.2 per cent of outputs from commercial models and 21.7 per cent from open-source models, a gap an attacker could exploit by publishing malicious packages under those names. The guidance recommends a short, ranked audit report that lists the location, reproduction steps, severity, and fix for each finding, with a retest column and a list of items that cannot be checked, such as third-party SaaS settings. Outside help is advised for apps that handle payments, health data, or LLM features with tool access, or where fundraising or an acquisition is imminent. The article does not name a single author for the guidance, and it closes by inviting readers to share their views.

Articles.Title: audit ai generated apps with seven security checks before production

stories.Headline: spotify doubles code changes with ai reviews quality controls
stories.Summary:
Spotify has more than doubled its monthly merged code changes, from about 8,100 to 17,000 year over year as of August, by expanding its use of AI-assisted development. The company has since been reviewing and adapting its quality and reliability controls to handle the larger volume of changes across its nearly 3,000 production services. The rise in volume prompted this review, and Spotify has identified problems in content processing, fleet changes, compute capacity, and mobile application quality. Spotify's own figures show that quality and optimisation work grew from 27 per cent to 31 per cent of merged changes, while maintenance and configuration fell from 31 per cent to 25 per cent. The company reported no matching rise in rework, though pull request size and code complexity are increasing.

The controls Spotify is changing cover monitoring, testing, rollout safeguards, rollback capacity, capacity planning, and quality measurement. After a June 24 incident in its content processing pipeline, which handles over 500,000 new items daily, the company added end-to-end monitoring, fixed a scheduling bug that had cut throughput by about 10 per cent, moved batch jobs to lower priority, and increased capacity. Episodes that normally appeared within minutes were delayed for hours during that incident. Spotify's Fleet Management system has merged over 2.5 million automated maintenance pull requests, most of them merged automatically after safety checks.

The company is also strengthening safeguards and expanding rollback capacity after an automated dependency upgrade passed existing checks but failed in production. It now schedules automated changes during the working hours of the teams that own the affected code. Spotify's incident review found no material direct contribution from AI-authored code, but it concluded that change volume had outpaced some verification controls. The company has described its own tools, including Honk, a background coding agent that runs Claude through the Agent SDK in Kubernetes pods, and Fleetshift, which handles target selection, scheduling, and progress tracking.

Google's 2025 DORA research, cited in the coverage, found that AI adoption is associated with higher software delivery throughput and product performance, but also with a negative relationship to delivery stability. That research points to automated testing, version control, and fast feedback loops as practices that matter as AI adoption grows. Spotify's reported response follows that direction. The articles do not say what further changes the company plans beyond those already described.

stories.Headline: bees ai agent desktop app architecture details revealed
stories.Summary:
Bees, an open-source desktop application for running AI agent teams locally, has had its architecture details revealed in an article published by TechGig on October 14, 2026. The app runs as three cooperating processes built on Tauri, Rust, and Node.js, with the Rust component handling the application window, tray, updater, and installer while supervising the other processes. When the window opens, it starts a local Temporal dev server and a bundled Node 24 runtime that hosts the DeepSeek Harness agent runtime. Temporal serves as the workflow engine, keeping work stages intact across restarts and backed by a SQLite file.

The Rust side keeps watch on the Node runtime and restarts it if it stops responding, returning the window to a splash screen in the meantime. A third process, llama-server from llama.cpp, runs only when local AI models are in use. Bees is built as plugins on top of the DeepSeek Harness, covering boards, schedules, and recovery, and it stores product data in a dedicated SQLite file called bees-stage1.db while keeping sensitive material such as file contents and credentials local. On restarts during tool calls, repeatable actions like reads and searches are run again, while non-repeatable actions such as sending an email pause the run for user review when their completion is uncertain, which prevents duplicates.

The article describes how the design choices were made by the Bees project, and it does not name individual people responsible for the code. According to the article, external models such as Claude Code and Codex are integrated by having Bees run their tools itself after strict JSON schema parsing, so the same permission checks apply to every model. Local models run through llama-server, with context windows sized according to system memory and GGUF file headers. File access is restricted to each run's folders, directories holding passwords or keys are blocked entirely, and every non-GET API request and data-sending browser step needs explicit approval, with that approval recorded in the run's audit events. The article reports these details without describing any next steps or future releases.

stories.Headline: supabase mcp server enables agents to provision backend infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Supabase, a Backend-as-a-Service platform, has introduced support for a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that lets AI agents provision and modify backend infrastructure directly. The company announced the feature at its Select 2026 event, and it was reported on October 14, 2026. Through the server, agents can set up database tables, change Row Level Security (RLS) policies, and deploy Edge Functions and long-running compute tasks without using the dashboard. Schema definitions are kept as SQL files, and changes flow back into version control, with migrations computed automatically by pg-delta. The server runs two separate authentication flows.

When an agent makes infrastructure changes on its own, it authenticates with project API keys that carry scoped permissions, and its actions are logged under an identifier distinct from human activity. When an agent running in a tool such as Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor works with an app, it acts as the signed-in user and is bound by the same RLS policies that apply in the web interface. Cost controls include an estimated cost in compute units returned before each query runs, configurable rate limits on each project API key, and project-level caps on runtime and memory. Tasks that exceed those caps are terminated, and the agent receives an error with resource usage details.

Agents cannot start long-running tasks beyond the caps without explicit human approval. When an agent generates a migration that conflicts with existing production data, the server returns a diff showing which columns or constraints would be dropped, how many rows would be affected, and whether the change can be rolled back safely. The agent can revise the migration, request human approval for destructive changes, or abort, and the check happens before anything runs. The server may also suggest safer options, such as adding a column rather than dropping one.

The articles say the company presents the design as making agents first-class consumers of backend infrastructure, and it describes the dual authentication model as preventing agents from bypassing application-level authorization. The articles do not say whether the feature is generally available or how widely it has been adopted, and they do not give pricing or cost figures beyond the compute-unit estimates. They also do not report any reaction from outside observers or independent testing of the controls. Supabase has not, according to the articles, indicated what further changes to the server are planned.

stories.Headline: langgraph guide for building production ready ai agents
stories.Summary:
A new guide published by TechGig on October 14, 2026 explains how to build reliable, stateful AI agents using LangGraph, an orchestration framework designed for agentic workflows. The guide describes LangGraph as offering explicit state management, native support for cycles and loops, first-class human-in-the-loop capabilities, and built-in checkpoints. It contrasts this with LangChain Agents, which rely on implicit state management and offer limited cycle support. The article was republished on October 25, 2026, at 5:00 UTC.

The core concepts are State, which serves as the single source of truth for the agent, and Nodes, which are functions that process the state and return updates. Edges and conditional routing govern how the agent moves between nodes. To illustrate, the guide walks through a complete example of a Research Assistant agent that plans, researches, and writes, using tools such as web search and a function that saves research notes. Advanced patterns covered include multi-agent collaboration, human-in-the-loop interactions, time-travel debugging, and structured output with validation.

The guide also offers a production checklist grouped under reliability, observability, and scaling. For reliability, it recommends checkpointing, error handling, timeouts, and rate limiting for external APIs. For observability, it points to LangSmith tracing, custom metrics for latency and token usage, and state logging. For scaling, it suggests horizontal scaling with stateless nodes and external checkpointing, queue-based execution for asynchronous node operations, and caching of large language model responses. Deployment options named include Docker, a FastAPI server, and Kubernetes.

The guide closes with testing and migration advice. Recommended testing includes unit tests for individual nodes, integration tests for the full graph, and property-based testing for diverse inputs. It also explains how existing LangChain Agents implementations can migrate to LangGraph using a drop-in replacement approach. The articles do not name a specific author for the guide or describe any plans for future updates.

stories.Headline: ai agent governance needs execution controls not just model checks
stories.Summary:
Banking regulators stepped up their scrutiny of autonomous AI agents on October 13, 2026, with a focus on how those agents gain access to production systems. The article argues that an agent holding production access without an enforceable limit on its authority amounts to an unbounded identity with credentials. It says traditional AI governance, which asks whether a model is accurate, fair, private and compliant, does not answer a harder question about what a production agent is permitted to do at a given moment. The piece contends that governance therefore has to cover the execution of actions, not just prompts and outputs. The framework it proposes requires binding each agent to its own identity and restricting the tools and data it can reach.

Risky actions should be intercepted before they run, results should be logged as evidence, and selected decisions should be escalated to people. The article describes agent governance as a runtime system of identity, permissions, policy enforcement, approval gates, audit evidence and shutdown controls. It says six controls matter most: agent identity, permissions, runtime policy, human approval, audit and containment. Agents should receive short-lived credentials, capped transaction values and limits on data classifications, and they should not inherit a developer's broad token.

The article puts the responsibility on the organisations that deploy these agents, and it points to the frameworks they can use to structure that work. It cites NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, which organises risk work around Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, and ISO/IEC 42001, which sets out an organisational AI management system. It describes both as voluntary or management-system guidance that must be turned into code paths, not left as policy documents. Its audit guidance calls for logs that record the agent's identity and version, the requesting principal, the requested action, the policy decision, approval state and the policy version that authorised each action.

Human approval, according to the article, should be required before actions with material financial, legal, security, privacy, customer or production impact, particularly when those actions are irreversible. The article frames these points as the current direction of enterprise practice rather than as settled regulation, and it does not describe any specific enforcement action or deadline. It concludes that the strongest approach is bounded autonomy with verifiable authority, in which agents act only within limits that can be proven after the fact. The article does not say what regulators will require next or when further guidance will arrive.

Articles.Title: ai agent governance needs execution controls not just model checks

stories.Headline: india sees 19 fold rise in forward deployed engineer job postings indeed data shows
stories.Summary:
Job postings for Forward Deployed Engineer roles in India rose almost 19-fold between June 2025 and June 2026, according to findings from the job site Indeed released on a Wednesday. Postings jumped 1,807 per cent year-on-year in June 2026, which Indeed says points to a deeper shift in how technology is deployed. The trend suggests companies are placing engineers closer to customers and their business problems. Demand eased after the June peak but stayed nearly 16 times higher year-on-year in July and more than six times higher in August.

The role combines technical skills with commercial and organisational abilities. Recent Glassdoor India listings ask for Python or Java, data engineering, machine learning, generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation, AI agents, cloud technologies, APIs and full-stack development. Employers also want stakeholder management, customer communication, problem-solving and collaboration with senior business and technology leaders. FDEs often act as a feedback loop, carrying customer problems to product teams and helping customers adopt new capabilities. Listings appear across technology companies, consulting firms, startups and specialist AI businesses, covering enterprise AI, data engineering, workflow automation and customer-service automation.

Sashi Kumar, Managing Director of Indeed India, said FDEs meet the need for engineers who can understand customer problems and put technology to work. He noted how quickly employers have adopted the role and said professionals need clearer information about the skills and career paths involved. Glassdoor India community discussions show professionals asking how FDE roles differ from traditional software engineering, along with questions about interview processes, required skills and work-life balance. Demand is emerging in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, New Delhi, Mumbai and remote locations.

Pay for the role is expected to sit at the higher end of software engineering compensation, though Indeed's sample is too small for a reliable median. Glassdoor India reports an average base pay of about ₹12 lakh a year for FDEs, with a range of ₹9 lakh to ₹16 lakh, based on 28 submissions as of January 2026. Glassdoor reports an average base pay of about ₹10 lakh a year for software engineers in India, based on a larger sample. Indeed Hiring Lab data also shows data centre job postings in India have nearly doubled over the last two years and now make up 1.3 per cent of all Indian job postings.

stories.Headline: top 5 cli coding agents for developers emerge post consolidation
stories.Summary:
The terminal-based AI development tool market consolidated sharply in 2026, prompting developers to review their toolchains. Google sunset its Gemini CLI on June 18, 2026, and SpaceX acquired Cursor in August, both of which pushed developers to reassess their options. The article, published on October 14, 2026, reports that the shift is driven by a desire for project independence, ownership of workflows, and resilient, private setups. The article names five leading agents that have emerged from the consolidation.

Command-line agents work directly within the shell, which gives them access to tools such as git, make, kubectl, and the file system. This lets them carry out complex jobs like multi-file refactoring and dependency updates. Claude Code, maintained by Anthropic, is described as an industry benchmark as of late 2026, and it supports the Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Fable 5.1 models. OpenAI Codex has moved to the GPT-6 series, is open source under the Apache-2.0 license, and offers a sandboxed execution mode. OpenCode works with any model provider, including Ollama and AWS Bedrock, and separates reading files from modifying them through distinct plan and build agents.

Cursor CLI, now owned by SpaceX, offers cloud handoff, which lets agents keep working in the cloud when the local machine is offline. Antigravity CLI is Google's replacement for the legacy Gemini CLI and is tied to the Antigravity 2.0 desktop platform, which keeps the terminal and graphical interface in sync. The article also gives practical guidance for using these agents. It recommends creating a new git branch before any agent edits the codebase, restricting the agent to relevant directories so the context window is not flooded, and configuring automatic test runs such as npm test or pytest after edits. It also points to the Model Context Protocol as a standard for connecting AI tools to services like Jira, Slack, and Notion.

stories.Headline: ai agents struggle with games excel at web development
stories.Summary:
AI agents perform well on web development work but struggle with game development, according to game programmer Kyle Kukshtel, as reported by TechGig on October 14, 2026. The reason, the report says, is that games contain many non-code elements that large language models cannot readily read, and game developers have far less training data for games than for web stacks. Kukshtel argues that the problem is mainly one of context management rather than a built-in limit of either LLMs or games. He suggests that making games more legible to AI agents is a matter of how the project is structured and presented to the model.

To address this, Kukshtel proposes several changes to how games are built. These include fixing randomness so the game state is deterministic, using image diffing so agents can reliably capture and compare screenshots, and adopting a "Thing-Driven Development" architecture in which every game entity is treated as a single object type. Paired with a command pattern, this lets agents change the game through serializable commands without recompiling it. The article also describes externalising game data from the code so agents can iterate on data changes more quickly, and a "Blackbox Game Architecture" that moves the simulation logic into its own library so it can be tested independently, including by AI agents.

Performance checks are also part of the approach. Kukshtel's approach uses profiling tools such as samply, which can export raw capture output as text that LLMs handle well, so agents can judge their own changes without a human reading the output. The report says the combined techniques can let an agentic development loop run through a change in seconds, speeding up iteration and improving the AI's grasp of game projects. The article presents these as strategies for improvement rather than a finished solution, and it does not describe any specific rollout or timeline for adoption. The main point it makes is that the gap between AI performance on web and game tasks may be narrowed by changing how game projects are organized.

Articles.Title: ai agents struggle with games excel at web development

stories.Headline: Oklahoma Local News Summit explores AI’s role in journalism
stories.Summary:
At an Oklahoma Local News Summit in Tulsa, journalists and media experts gathered to discuss how artificial intelligence is reshaping reporting, with concerns about accuracy, public records access and press freedoms at the center of the conversation. The event was organized by Freedom of Information Oklahoma, the Oklahoma Media Center and the Oklahoma Pro Chapter of the Society of Professional Journalists, and coverage was published on October 23, 2026. A panel titled "Are We Truly Free 250 Years Later?" was moderated by Griffin Media's Scott Mitchell and examined how AI and political polarization are affecting First Amendment freedoms. Three speakers joined the discussion: Leslie Briggs, Oklahoma attorney for the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press; Wendy Suares, evening anchor and investigative journalist at KOKH Fox 25; and Mark Thomas, executive vice president of the Oklahoma Press Association.

The panelists described both the promise and the risks of the technology. Briggs pointed to a Pulitzer Prize-winning investigation into missing persons cases in Chicago, produced by a journalist with the Invisible Institute, which used machine learning to analyze more than one million public records and documents. She also warned that government agencies could use AI to answer public records requests in ways that shield information, since the models can be steered toward particular search results. Suares said AI cannot replicate the human judgment, relationships and context that reporters bring, but it can help sift records and court cases for new developments. Thomas urged journalists not to let the ease of AI replace the hard work of reporting.

The panel also raised the question of copyright and policy. Briggs asked where the line falls between copyrightable work and output produced by analyzing large volumes of documents, and she suggested that the issue may need to be addressed at the federal level. Thomas framed the broader purpose of journalism as seeking and telling the truth so communities can make informed decisions about daily life, from voting to road closures. The articles do not report any specific policy proposal, legislative action or ruling that emerged from the summit, and they do not describe next steps beyond the discussion itself.

Articles.Title: Oklahoma Local News Summit explores AI’s role in journalism

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence and advanced computer vision to recover more textile waste
stories.Summary:
Tecnalia, a Spanish research and technology organisation, has announced that it has developed and validated a technology that combines advanced computer vision and artificial intelligence to automatically identify and sort textile waste under real conditions. The work is part of the CIRTEXCAM initiative and was carried out with the company Valoriza, with the announcement published on 23 October 2026. The system uses a mix of sensors, including RGB imaging, near-infrared (NIR) imaging and 3D imaging, to gather complementary information about each item of waste. Its purpose is to detect, identify and characterise textile waste so that it can be sorted and recovered more effectively.

The article explains that greater circularity in the textile sector depends on more than better recycling technology, because materials must first be properly identified, sorted and prepared. It notes that the wide variety of garments, compositions and formats, together with other waste mixed in, makes textile sorting difficult and limits reuse and recycling. To test the technology, the team ran a pilot at a waste management plant in collaboration with Valoriza, working with pre-sorted textiles, non-textile waste and combinations of both. Footwear waste was also added to make the tests more complex. The pilot was designed to assess performance in conditions similar to those a future industrial solution would face and to generate new datasets for improving the artificial intelligence models.

The article attributes the work to Tecnalia, and its author is listed as Nerea Campos. The organisation says the aim goes beyond sorting pre-separated materials to also identifying textiles that currently go unnoticed and are often left out of reuse or recycling processes. It describes the combination of sensing, computer vision and artificial intelligence as a way to automate textile waste recovery and increase the supply of materials for a more circular economy. The article presents this as a step toward recovering materials that are still being lost today. It does not state a timeline for an industrial rollout, and it gives no further details on next steps beyond continuing to improve and validate the models.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence and advanced computer vision to recover more textile waste

Their position, as the description presents it, is that AI needs to be used responsibly. The page does not spell out what responsible use would require, and it does not set out any rules, limits or policy changes. Beyond the author himself, the articles do not identify anyone formally responsible or record any statement from the author, the publisher or an industry body.

The description attributes the views to unnamed artists and academics, so it is not possible to say who holds which position. stories.Headline: ai agent toolchains consolidate skill registry for governance needed
stories.Summary:
AI toolchains are consolidating, according to recent GitHub Trending projects that were reported on October 14, 2026, and the trend has led to a call for a governance layer in multi-agent workflows. One project, Alishahryar1/free-claude-code, brings more than 10 AI coding assistants, including Claude Code, Codex, and VSCode, under a single entry point. Another, mksglu/context-mode, adds context window optimisation, session memory persistence, and enforced routing across 17 platforms. A third, morluto/rea, shows that agent chains can handle deep engineering work such as native binary reverse engineering.

The article argues that this consolidation follows a pattern of unifying, governing, and then executing, but that a gap remains in skill registries and governance. Without them, it is hard to know who can call which skill, which version is running, and what happened when a skill was invoked. Developers are therefore urged to implement skill registries that manage permissions, versions, and audit trails. The article points to iflytek/skillhub as one answer, an open-source, self-hosted skill registry for AI agents that offers package publishing with version management, Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) permissions, and audit logs for every skill invocation.

The article describes this kind of registry as one layer of a complete stack for agent workflows. Alongside unified entry points, context routing, and skill governance, the stack also includes workflow orchestration, which it cites as astron-agent, and execution through agent chains, cited as rea. The piece presents these tools as examples drawn from GitHub Trending rather than as a survey of the wider market. It does not describe any regulatory requirement or formal industry standard for skill registries. It also does not say what, if anything, follows next for these projects beyond their current availability.

stories.Headline: seven steps to integrate ai into existing applications
stories.Summary:
The TechGig article, published on October 25, 2026, lays out a seven-step plan for adding AI to software that already exists, and it argues that most of these projects fail because of backend plumbing rather than weak model performance. It opens by describing the approach as a structured engineering process centered on stability and security. The first step is to pick one narrow use case and define how it can fail, such as summarizing a support ticket with a clear input and output. The article also notes that the piece was first posted on October 14, 2026, while the metadata lists October 25.

The remaining steps focus on how the system is built. The model should sit behind the company's own backend so the browser or mobile app calls the company's API, which then calls the model, keeping keys and usage limits under control. Every model call should be wrapped in a timeout, retries, and a fallback, since SDKs from OpenAI and Anthropic ship with long default timeouts that the article considers unsuitable for user-facing requests. Answers should be grounded in the company's own data through retrieval-augmented generation, with documents filtered by user permissions before the model sees them. Output should be constrained and validated, for example with OpenAI's Structured Outputs using a JSON Schema, and the feature should be secured against the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, 2025 edition.

The article attributes this guidance to its own engineering recommendations and identifies no specific organization as responsible for a single event. It advises teams to set monthly spend limits, use caching, and log request IDs and token usage to control cost and monitor performance. It recommends rolling out features behind a feature flag with a kill switch and considering shadow mode testing, which scores real traffic without showing results to users. It says specialist help is advisable for integrations with CRM, ERP, or payment systems, for regulated data, or where a team lacks retrieval pipeline experience. The article also includes a commercial mention of Dev Technosys, a Jaipur-based firm that offers a seven-stage AI integration process and reports ISO 27001:2022, ISO 9001:2015, and CMMI Level 3 credentials.

Articles.Title: seven steps to integrate ai into existing applications

stories.Headline: building ai agents with function calling a complete guide
stories.Summary:
A new guide published on TechGig on October 14, 2026 lays out how to build production-ready AI agents using function calling. The guide explains how this technique lets large language models execute code, call APIs, query databases, and interact with external systems, turning them from text generators into action-taking agents. It covers architecture, validation, error handling, and deployment patterns for building these agents robustly. The source article is dated October 25, 2026 in its metadata. The proposed architecture has three stages.

First, an LLM analyzes a user request and decides whether a function call is needed. If one is, a Function Executor validates and runs the call and returns the result. Finally, the LLM writes a response based on that outcome. The guide shows how Python functions can be turned into JSON Schema definitions automatically, giving the model a clear contract for each tool. A FunctionRegistry class handles registering functions, retrieving their schemas, and executing them across categories such as code, network, data, research, and filesystem operations.

The core loop lives in a FunctionCallingAgent class that works with an AsyncOpenAI client and keeps the conversation history as it cycles through model calls, tool executions, and response generation. Safety is handled by several parts: a FunctionValidator checks arguments against their schemas, an OutputValidator allows custom checks on results, and a PythonSandbox runs Python code in a contained environment. The guide also covers parallel function execution for handling several calls at once, function composition for chaining operations into pipelines, and function call tracing to monitor performance, success rates, and errors. Its best practices stress single responsibility, idempotency, explicit contracts, robust failure handling, and thorough security in function design. The articles provided do not say who wrote the guide or whether it is tied to any company or product, and they do not describe its reception or any planned follow-up.

Articles.Title: building ai agents with function calling a complete guide

stories.Headline: ai engineer nyc workshops target agent evaluations finance orchestration
stories.Summary:
AI Engineer NYC opened with a day of 18 hands-on workshops, designed to give attendees practical experience with the challenges of building AI systems. Seven of the sessions focused on agent evaluations, which address how to prove that an AI agent actually works. Laurie Voss taught "Evaluations with Phoenix 101," SallyAnn DeLucia led "AI Evaluation 101," and Xander Song introduced Harbor for shipping agents based on evidence rather than intuition. Sessions from Sonar and Langfuse, along with a workshop led by Nick Nisi and Zack Proser, also stressed the need to define when an agent is considered finished.

Six workshops targeted financial services and other regulated industries, including one on a wealth management concierge and another on an anti-money laundering agent. According to the coverage, these sessions highlighted the need for audit trails and for handling complex, unstructured data inside regulated environments. A third group of workshops covered model orchestration, permissions, reliability, and cost. Topics included orchestrating Claude Managed Agents, building self-improving agents, and securing long-running agents with Keycard and Temporal.

Eugene Cheah's "Tokenomics 101" dealt with the costs involved in running AI agents. The workshops were reported to have been held on the first day of the conference, which the coverage described as an effort to focus on hands-on, practical learning. The articles do not name a sponsor or organizer beyond the conference itself, and they do not describe any outcomes or follow-up events. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services published a hands-on guide on October 23, 2026, explaining how to run Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI. The method trains a model on tasks that involve a sequence of actions, where the only feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which calls the policy model being trained, acts over as many turns as the task requires, and returns a single reward when the episode ends. The guide uses the word game Wordle as its example, because its rules are simple and its outcomes can be scored objectively.

The pipeline depends on two IAM roles and a deployed agent. The agent runtime role trusts bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com and carries the AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess managed policy, while the training job role must trust job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com with both sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession. The author warns that using the generic sagemaker.amazonaws.com principal makes job creation fail with a "Could not assume role" error. The agent is deployed with the AgentCore command line tool, and the guide recommends that route over uploading a code package in the console. Training uses Group Relative Policy Optimization to update a Low-Rank Adaptation adapter, and the reward gives 1.05 to 1.55 for a solve depending on speed, -0.5 for a loss, and -1.5 for never making a valid guess.

In the authors' run, the method raised gpt-oss-20b's solve rate on held-out words from 61 to 84 percent at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at. The 100-step run cost about $339 in training tokens across 105,486 rollouts over 12 hours and 40 minutes, plus roughly $79 in AgentCore runtime charges. The guide says the training stage accounts for most of the token cost and scales with trajectory length. It also says the trained data, agent and model remain in the user's AWS account and are not used to train the base models. The service is offered for Amazon Nova 2 Lite, GPT-OSS-20B, Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.6 27B, in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon), though the article states that the Region list may change.

Articles.Title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide

stories.Headline: Enterprises face evolving insurance landscape for artificial intelligence risks
stories.Summary:
Insurers are increasingly weighing how to cover artificial intelligence risks, according to a brief from SC Media published on October 23, 2026, which draws on reporting from Dark Reading. The piece says enterprises are seeking coverage for potential harms from rogue AI agents and automated system failures, and that the insurance market has not settled on how to respond. Some specialty firms sell purpose-built policies or affirmative endorsements that address these threats directly. Many large carriers, however, are adding strict exclusions to their policies.

Major insurers named in the brief, including Chubb, Travelers and AIG, have adopted Verisk/ISO endorsement language that limits their liability for damages tied to generative AI. The article notes that this leaves many organizations exposed, since standard cyber or errors and omissions policies often do not cover these emerging threats. Experts quoted in the reporting advise companies to carry out thorough policy reviews to find gaps in their current protection. Companies that want specialized coverage are expected to show strong security controls, and underwriters are paying closer attention to how businesses monitor their AI applications. The article says underwriters treat these applications much like critical service accounts.

The brief places responsibility for closing these gaps mainly with the enterprises themselves, which must demonstrate guardrails, human oversight and supply chain management to qualify for better terms. It says executives need to deal with shadow AI, meaning unsanctioned AI use inside the organization, and to secure infrastructure, data pipelines and third-party contracts against both malicious attacks and non-malicious system failures. The reporting attributes these recommendations to experts and underwriting practice rather than to any single regulator. The article does not report any formal rule change or deadline. Its framing is that the insurance landscape for AI remains in flux, with coverage terms likely to keep shifting as adoption grows.

Articles.Title: Enterprises face evolving insurance landscape for artificial intelligence risks

stories.Headline: CISA, Allies Warn of Denial-of-Wallet Risks in AI Token Guidance
stories.Summary:
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and four allied cyber agencies released joint guidance on a Thursday in October 2026 to help organizations keep artificial intelligence token consumption from inflating costs, exhausting service quotas and disrupting critical services. The guidance, titled "Managing AI Token Consumption for Operational Resilience," was published by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and co-authored by CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre, and the national cyber security centers of New Zealand and the United Kingdom. The agencies said usage-based AI pricing is hard to forecast and that token demand will rise as AI becomes more embedded in operations. They noted that agentic workflows, which reprocess earlier content at each step, add to that demand. The guidance proposes a three-tier model for allocating AI capacity.

Cyber defense and incident response sit at the top tier, compliance, policy analysis and other core business functions form a monitored middle tier, and routine productivity tasks such as email drafting could be throttled when demand peaks. The agencies acknowledged that reserving capacity for the top tier adds cost but said the tradeoff strengthens continuity. The document also describes denial-of-tokens attacks, which aim to lock out legitimate users by burning through an organization's token supply or tripping its rate limits. A related tactic, denial-of-wallet, targets an organization's budget through complex queries or loops that force a model to repeatedly process its own output. The agencies suggested feeding token telemetry into security information and event management platforms, since unusual spikes may also signal data exfiltration.

The agencies advised organizations to learn how token pricing works before committing to service-level agreements and to evaluate providers on reliability and quota constraints. They also recommended spreading workloads across multiple providers so they can be rerouted during outages, and matching smaller or locally run models to simpler tasks. Critical infrastructure operators were urged to keep manual fallbacks ready in case AI becomes unavailable. The publication follows joint guidance on securely adopting agentic AI services that intelligence and cybersecurity agencies from the same five countries released in May, which outlined privilege, behavior and accountability risks tied to autonomous AI agents.

Articles.Title: CISA, Allies Warn of Denial-of-Wallet Risks in AI Token Guidance

Agent Yvonne Faustinos explains that AI is simplifying many of her daily tasks, which gives her more time to connect with buyers and sellers. stories.Headline: PHP Warning Highlights Battle Between AI Speed, Cyber Hygiene
stories.Summary:
On October 21, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued an urgent alert about a pair of web server vulnerabilities known as php2shell. The flaws affect the PHP programming language, which reportedly runs on about 70 percent of the world's websites, and could let an intruder run code on an affected server without logging in and steal or alter data. CISA said it had not observed exploitation as of the time of publication, but warned that unpatched systems remained at risk. Security researchers at Wiz and Calif used Google Gemini and OpenAI models to find the flaws, which they said had been present for decades across multiple PHP versions.

CISA directed organizations to immediately update their PHP code on internet-facing systems, or take those systems offline until they could be patched. Reports said some government services were taken down in countries including the United Kingdom, Japan and Finland. No federal government websites in the United States reported outages from php2shell, though one security executive cautioned that a site still running does not mean it is secure. The article also describes CISA's broader shift toward faster remediation, including a risk-based approach that gives agencies no more than three days to deploy patches for serious mitigations. The agency has also rolled out a cloud-based monitoring platform, Security Information and Event Management-as-a-service, through its Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation program.

David Williams, founder and CEO of the UK-based Fior Group, said the immediate priorities are patching, investigating possible compromise and replacing exposed credentials. He argued that governments should design security on the assumption that some vulnerabilities will be exploited before they can be patched, and that the key question is what an attacker can do once inside. Katie Chrisman, federal solutions engineering team lead at NinjaOne, said at a GovCIO Media & Research forum on October 8 that three days should be seen as a new baseline, and that the organizations that succeed will be those that patch quickly while also trusting their underlying data. A CISA spokesperson said on Friday that the agency had no information beyond its October 21 alert.

The episode shows how AI is changing the pace of both attack and defense. Because the technology can locate weaknesses far faster than before, it has also removed the resource constraints that once kept attackers from finding long-standing flaws, so officials must now patch and monitor for exploits on a much shorter timeline. The article does not say whether any exploitation has since been confirmed or what further guidance CISA may issue. It also does not say whether the three-day patching requirement applies to php2shell specifically. More to follow.

Articles.Title: PHP Warning Highlights Battle Between AI Speed, Cyber Hygiene

stories.Headline: REDESCA Calls for the Protection of Labor Rights in the Face of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation
stories.Summary:
The Special Rapporteurship on Economic, Social, Cultural, and Environmental Rights (REDESCA) of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights issued a press release on October 23, 2026, calling for stronger public policies and rules so that the spread of artificial intelligence, algorithmic management, and other digital tools in work respects human rights. The office says these changes can raise productivity and open new economic activities, but they can also widen inequality, create new forms of precarious work, and weaken the effective exercise of basic rights. REDESCA notes that automated systems are already used in hiring, task assignment, supervision, performance evaluation, pay, and dismissal in both the private and public sectors. It warns that such use can affect the right to fair working conditions, social security, health, equality, privacy, freedom of expression, freedom of association, and collective bargaining. The office also says that access to effective protection and redress must be guaranteed.

REDESCA states that the duties to respect, protect, and guarantee human rights apply to the design, acquisition, and use of new technologies at work, and it points to the American Convention on Human Rights, the Protocol of San Salvador, and IACHR and Inter-American Court standards as guidance. It calls for transparency that gives workers and their representatives understandable information they can use to verify, negotiate, and challenge decisions. The office also urges safeguards against disproportionate surveillance, improper use of personal data, algorithmic discrimination, and automated decisions that lack clear explanations, meaningful human review, or appeal mechanisms. It says governments need integrated policies covering labor law, data protection, equality, occupational safety and health, social protection, and corporate responsibility. Public institutions, in its view, should be able to identify which systems are in use, access documentation, audit their operation, and order corrective measures.

REDESCA also stresses that workers and their organizations, through social dialogue and collective bargaining, must take part in these responses. The office draws attention to Latin America and the Caribbean, where high levels of informality, outsourcing, non-standard employment, structural inequality, and limited social protection can magnify the risks, with women and migrants facing disproportionate effects. It says training, retraining, protection against unfair shifting of risks and arbitrary loss of income, and fair sharing of productivity gains must be part of a just digital transition. In this context, REDESCA describes the adoption in June 2026 of International Labour Organization Convention No. 193 on Decent Work in the Platform Economy as significant, since it is the first international labor standard dedicated to this issue. According to the office, the convention addresses labor rights, automated management systems, personal data, compensation, social security, and review of certain automated decisions, and it will serve as a reference once it is ratified and enters into force.

REDESCA also notes that a technical workshop it held with the Special Rapporteurship on Freedom of Expression during the 196th Session in August 2026 examined these issues, and that it will support a side event at the 197th Session in Panama. REDESCA says it will keep contributing, within its mandate and in coordination with other IACHR bodies, to analysis of how digital transformation affects economic, social, cultural, and environmental rights. It calls for continued dialogue with states, workers' organizations, civil society, businesses, international bodies, and academics on monitoring, technical cooperation, research, and regional discussion. The office frames the goal as a digital transition that is just, inclusive, and respectful of human rights. The Special Rapporteurship is an office of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, which is an autonomous principal organ of the Organization of American States.

Articles.Title: REDESCA Calls for the Protection of Labor Rights in the Face of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation

stories.Headline: developers guide to voice cloning technology with elevenlabs api
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news event. The article is a how-to guide published on TechGig on October 14, 2026, which the site lists as October 25 in its metadata, and it explains how developers can use the ElevenLabs API to build voice cloning into their own software. It describes voice AI as moving from research into everyday products such as virtual assistants, podcast generators, and accessibility tools. Because the piece is instructional rather than a report on an incident, there is no single event, actor, or decision to report.

The guide walks through the technical steps. Voice cloning produces synthetic speech that copies a speaker's timbre, accent, and style, and modern systems rely on neural networks trained on short audio samples. Building such a system from scratch needs large datasets, GPU clusters, and audio expertise, so the article presents a hosted API as the more practical route. According to the piece, ElevenLabs supports real-time streaming synthesis, custom cloning from minimal audio, multiple languages, and WebSocket connections for low-latency use. Developers install the Python SDK, create an API key, and clone a voice by supplying a WAV or MP3 file, typically 16kHz mono audio.

The article also covers adjusting speed, pitch, emotion, and volume during generation, and shows how a Flask web application can expose a /speak endpoint that turns text into speech using a chosen voice ID. It raises ethical concerns, including consent, attribution, and the risk of deep-fake audio used for misinformation. It advises developers to get explicit permission from speakers, disclose synthetic voices, and use ElevenLabs' compliance framework for voice data and consent workflows. Production practices it recommends include caching embeddings, rate limiting keys, batching requests, and monitoring usage for anomalies. The article does not describe any ongoing developments or next steps beyond these recommendations.

Articles.Title: developers guide to voice cloning technology with elevenlabs api

stories.Headline: Did Texas use artificial intelligence to call fourth-down play against Florida?
stories.Summary:
A report from the Austin American-Statesman said that during the fourth quarter of Texas's game against Florida at Royal-Memorial Stadium, the Longhorns used a new artificial intelligence data analytics platform called Bevo Lab to help decide a fourth-down play. Trailing 20-17 and facing fourth-and-2, coach Steve Sarkisian and his staff reportedly turned to the tool. Texas failed to convert after quarterback Arch Manning lost three yards on the play. The report appeared on a Friday, the same day the school announced the Bevo Lab, a 25,000-square-foot AI facility on campus. The announcement describes the lab as a space where artificial intelligence informs coaching decisions and daily athletic department work, and the school has been building tools with Google for areas such as revenue-sharing and roster management.

The Statesman report framed the fourth-down moment as a pivotal use of that new technology. Fans reacted quickly on social media, many of them suggesting the coaches had simply asked an AI which play to run. The article notes that the frustration followed consecutive losses to unranked teams and an underwhelming season from Manning. Athletic Director Chris Del Conte responded roughly an hour after the report was published, telling Bobby Burton that the story was wrong in its implication. He said the decision to go for it on fourth-and-2 was not based on Bevo Lab analysis.

Del Conte explained that he had used the play only as an example of what the platform could suggest, not of what it actually did during the game. The outlet's reporter also argued that the fan speculation was overblown and that Sarkisian was not likely reading AI-generated instructions to Manning. The episode comes as Texas prepares to face Ole Miss on Saturday night, with the team's season under scrutiny. The articles do not report any further investigation or any formal response beyond Del Conte's clarification. They also do not say whether the Statesman will issue a correction or update its reporting.

Articles.Title: Did Texas use artificial intelligence to call fourth-down play against Florida?

stories.Headline: vkore enables lora training on inference only npus
stories.Summary:
VKORE, a software acceleration layer developed by VIDRAFT, now allows LoRA training of transformer models on NPUs that were typically designated for inference-only tasks. The announcement was published by TechGig on October 14, 2026, at 11:30 PM IST. The same layer raised single-user inference speed by 3.8 times and server throughput by 4.1 times on the same NPU server. Measurements were made on a Korean NPU server with eight cards and 32 chips, using Google's open Gemma 4 26B model.

During LoRA training, VKORE achieved 0.9999 numerical parity with standard PyTorch. Training on the NPU ran roughly 170 times faster than on the same server's CPU. The reported gains matter because they challenge the usual data centre economics, which typically separate GPUs for training from NPUs for inference. If the claims hold, operators could run fine-tuning on existing NPU inference fleets during low-traffic hours. That would remove the need for separate GPU infrastructure for fine-tuning tasks.

VIDRAFT is the developer named in the reporting, and the article presents VKORE as a hardware-independent layer for data centres that use both GPUs and NPUs. The figures come from the developer's own measurements on a single Korean server, and the article does not report independent verification. The piece also does not say whether VKORE is commercially available or when it might be. Further details on availability, testing beyond the one server, and deployment plans were not included in the article.
